CORRECTION to the median-per-key hypothesis recorded one batch ago at romans 8. That note proposed median under ~400 predicts a tileable register chapter and over ~1,000 predicts per-verse comment, with the 400-1,000 band untested and flagged as needing a case. Whatever boundary exists is therefore much lower and much narrower than proposed, and a median in the low hundreds is nowhere near sufficient evidence on its own. The measure that actually worked in both cases was the ADJACENCY CHECK — read three to five consecutive keys and ask whether they say the same procedural thing. On numbers 3 that showed a five-slot template repeated verbatim for three houses; on genesis 31 it showed five consecutive verses of one speech drawing 22, 103, 169, 411 and 782 words, which is the signature of distinct content. CORRECTION to my own note of earlier today: the claim that 'keys already >=350 source words set a hard floor on entry count, since those verses cannot be grouped without manufacturing padding' is WRONG, and leviticus 13 falsifies it. This chapter has 20 keys at 350+ yet tiles cleanly into 10 pericope entries. The reasoning was backwards: a THIN key cannot reach 350 output words honestly and so MUST be grouped, but a fat key merely CAN stand alone — it does not have to, and grouping fat keys just means the writer selects from more material than one entry needs (numbers 3 collapsed spans of 900-3000 source words into single entries). So keys>=350 is not a floor on entries and should not be used as a batch-sizing trigger. The other worker's n>2k metric is a different and better-founded claim and is not affected by this correction. What actually predicts entry count remains the genre regime, established by the adjacency check: leviticus 13 is the textbook regime (b)/(c) case, a priestly diagnostic manual whose nine natural sections (the examination, old leprosy, the boil, the burn, the scall, the harmless spot, the bald head, the leper's conduct, garments) tile 1-59 exactly with every span over 800 source words.

The over-writing problem is now measured rather than guessed, and it is the dominant cost of this loop. Targets and outcomes across four chapters: genesis 41 target 650, first draft ~1,330/entry; leviticus 13 target 500, first draft ~900; exodus 9 target 450, first draft ~900. The target has almost no effect on the draft — output has landed near 900-1,300 words per entry regardless, because the writing method is 'cover every voice's every point' and the spans carry 2,000-4,500 source words. Trimming back to 350-650 then costs more passes than the writing did (this chapter took roughly 30 edit rounds). Two things that did work and should be standard: (1) deleting a whole paragraph beats shortening sentences, since sentence-level trimming yields about 15% per pass and the gap is routinely 35%; (2) when a paragraph goes, its tag lines must go with it — several stale debates and outliers survived a deletion here and had to be pruned afterwards. The named-but-not-sourced check caught a real misattribution I would otherwise have shipped. Writing entry 3-9 I reproduced Henry's survey of the competing reconstructions of the troop numbers, which includes the clause 'as Calvin thinks, he kept entire for that purpose'. That is Henry CITING Calvin; Calvin has no block of his own in vv3-9. Naming Calvin there would have credited him with a position in a span where the corpus carries nothing from him. Rephrased to 'on another reckoning Henry reports'. General rule: when a commentator names another commentator inside his own block, that is quotation, not a second voice — attribute it to the quoting author or leave it unnamed.

JFB scrape residue, tenth chapter — and the first time the drift stays INSIDE the same book. All four JFB blocks in exodus 21 carry Exodus 8-9 plagues material (the frogs and the Nile, the bargain to sacrifice within the land, the murrain announced to Pharaoh, the brick-kiln and the boils). Legal chapters tile more cheaply than narrative but cost the same to write. Exodus 21 is regime (b): 36 verses of case law falling into five clean pericopes (1-6, 7-11, 12-17, 18-27, 28-36) at 20,641 source words, so the tiling was obvious in a way judges 9 never was. But the per-entry writing cost was no lower — every entry still needed two trim passes from 740-900 words, because legal material multiplies SHORT independent claims (a rendering, a rabbinic gloss, a Roman parallel, a case distinction) rather than long ones, and short claims are exactly what resists compression: you cannot drop half a case distinction. Practical note for sizing: source words per chapter predicts reading cost well, but the number of distinct adjudicated points predicts writing cost better, and legal chapters run high on the second measure even when low on the first.

Two commentators use racial language in this chapter that a modern reader will hit head-on: Clarke on the manstealing law (v16) names the contemporary slave trade in period terms, and Wesley on the beaten servant (v20) glosses the Gentile slave by direct comparison with enslaved people on colonial plantations. Both are making arguments the synthesis should carry — Clarke is CONDEMNING the trade and holding the purchaser as guilty as the thief, which is the substance worth preserving — so I rendered the substance and dropped the period vocabulary rather than quoting it. Recording the decision because it is a judgement call another worker will face: the rule I applied is that where the dated term is incidental to the argument, paraphrase it; where a commentator's own prejudice IS the claim, that would need flagging as a source-defect instead, not silent laundering. Neither case here was the latter.

Two entries here came in at 449 and 445 words against source spans of 1,921 and 1,004 words, and the audit gave them no PAD, THIN or FLOOR flag — mean TTR 0.656. This is worth recording because the loop's habit is to aim near the 650 ceiling regardless of how much source a span carries, which is exactly what drives the trim spiral. Sizing the TARGET to the span rather than to the window produced clean entries on the first pass and no trimming at all for three of this chapter's four entries. Suggested rule: pick a per-entry target of roughly source-words divided by four to eight depending on density, then check it against the 350-650 window, instead of defaulting to the ceiling. A thin span honestly written at 430 words scores better than the same span padded to 620.

BLOCKED — psalms 108 cannot be synthesised under the current rules and needs an owner decision, like numbers 31. Its cow source is missing keys 5, 8 and 12 entirely, so the present keys fall into four contiguous runs: 1-4 (2,209 source words), 6-7 (1,503), 9-11 (75) and 13 (303). validate-synthesis.py rejects any pericope covering a verse absent from the source ('entries cover verses absent from the source: [5, 8, 12]'), so spans cannot bridge the gaps; but the 9-11 and 13 runs cannot honestly support the 350-word floor, 9-11 having only 75 usable source words across three verses. Every legal tiling therefore requires padding. Two possible fixes, both owner calls: re-scrape or repair the source so that 5, 8 and 12 are present, or relax the tiling rule to let a pericope span verses the source is silent on (which is arguably the right reading anyway, since a pericope is a unit of the text, not of the commentary). I drafted and measured both entries for a 1-5 / 6-13 tiling before hitting the validator, and reverted rather than pad or work around the gate. Worth a corpus-wide scan for other chapters whose cow source has interior key gaps — this is the first I have hit, but nothing suggests it is unique.

Period-prejudice handling, two instances, both handled by the rule recorded at exodus 21 (render the substance, drop the vocabulary, flag it here). Calvin at v3 opens 'Here the vanity of the female disposition appears' - his exegetical claim is that Rachel sought a triumph by illicit arts instead of fleeing to God, and the generalisation about women is his framing, not the argument; rendered the claim without it. Calvin at v14 grounds the meanness of the narrative in a generalisation about Jewish boasting in ancestry - the argument (a humble origin recorded to humble pride and exalt grace) stands without the ethnic target, and was rendered that way. Fourth clean chapter running under the span-sized-target rule: genesis 30 spans of 6998/4901/7331/5377 source words gave entries of 650/649/644/648. The chapter is unusually voice-dense (seven commentators on nearly every key, four schools throughout), and dense spans push drafts well over the ceiling even when the target is set correctly. Suggest the rule be stated as source-words divided by 4-8 BY VOICE COUNT, tightening toward the low end when six or more voices are live.

The numbers 31 blocker is STRUCTURAL, not specific to that chapter, and 28 other chapters share it. Corpus scan: 61 chapters have interior gaps in their cow source keys. Of those, 29 contain at least one contiguous run of present keys too thin to support the 350-word prose floor (using <900 usable source words as the threshold). validate-synthesis.py rejects any pericope covering a verse absent from the source, so spans cannot bridge the gaps; a run like numbers 31's 42-42 (211 source words) or psalms 108's 9-11 (75 words across three verses) therefore has no legal, unpadded tiling under the new format. All 29 are currently DONE only because they hold LEGACY per-verse synthesis — one prose string per source key, no ranges — which satisfies the tiling rule trivially. numbers 31 has exactly 42 entries for its 42 source keys. Every one of these will hit the same wall the moment it is repaired into the pericope format. The 29: 1chronicles 1,2,6,8,9,16,25; 1corinthians 16; deuteronomy 14; exodus 35,36,37,38,39; ezra 2,8,10; galatians 2; luke 3; nehemiah 7,10,11,12; numbers 26,28,29,31,34; psalms 108 (the only one not yet synthesised at all). Two fixes, both owner calls, and one decision covers all 29: repair the sources so the missing keys are present, or relax the tiling rule to let a pericope span verses the commentary is silent on — the latter being arguably correct anyway, since a pericope is a unit of the text and not of the commentary. Note that some gaps are large and clearly scrape losses: exodus 36 is missing 10-13, 15-18, 21-25, 27-29, 33-34, 36; nehemiah 7 is missing more verses than it has.

See the numbers 31 note filed the same day: psalms 108 is one of 29 chapters blocked by interior source-key gaps, and the only one of the 29 with no synthesis at all yet. It is therefore the cheapest test case for whichever fix is chosen — two entries drafted and measured to a 1-5 / 6-13 tiling are all that is needed once the rule or the source changes.

Third of the repeated psalms handled in this run, after psalms 70 (= psalms 40:13-17) and psalms 108 (= psalms 57 + 60). The pattern holds and is worth stating once for whoever repairs psalms 14: every voice declines to expound psalms 53 afresh and refers back — Calvin says a distinct commentary is unnecessary, Clarke sends the reader to his notes on the fourteenth and adds only short remarks, Henry says the psalm was opened before and confines himself to three observations on sin. What is left is largely a variant list, so the synthesis is heavier in textual comparison and lighter in doctrine than a normal chapter. Keil and Delitzsch supply the one substantive argument: the divine name occurs seven times in both recensions, mingled deliberately as Elohim and Jahve in psalms 14 but levelled to Elohim throughout here, more rigidly than the Elohimic character demands, from which they conclude David cannot himself have made the change. psalms 14 is the last of this family still unhandled.

JFB residue, sixteenth chapter: all seven blocks are Genesis 24 material (Rebekah unveiled at the well, the nose-ring and armlets, the servant declining food till he had told his errand). FOURFOLD DUPLICATION: keys 23, 29, 35 and 41 carry the SAME 29-word block, byte-identical. judges 1 gave the first exact duplicate at two keys; this is four. So the corruption is not a one-block-per-key displacement at all - a single intruding block can be stamped across many keys in one file. Any dedup pass must treat repetition within a chapter as expected, not anomalous.

EDITORIAL DISSENT EMBEDDED IN CALVIN'S BLOCKS, twice in one chapter. At v5, inside Calvin's own block, an editor interrupts: 'This is a dangerous position, however it may be modified or explained. True faith never leads to sin... What Calvin calls zeal, he ought to have called rashness and something worse.' At v11 again: 'There is a great want of Calvin's accustomed caution and soundness in all this reasoning... It is much more probable that Jacob was influenced by a precipitate and ambitious desire...'. These are the translator/editor arguing WITH Calvin inside the block a synthesiser would naturally read as Calvin's. I attributed only Calvin's own claims. Anyone building an attribution checker needs to know the Calvin text in this corpus carries a second, contrary voice under the same heading.

K&D blocks that are bare verse quotation with no comment, twice in one chapter (v6 and the v31/v33 run), both excluded via EXCL_BY_ENTRY rather than forced into a mention. Meanwhile the v19/v25 K&D block DID carry one usable clause buried in the quotation. The working rule stands: check the quotation for a trailing comment before excluding, but do not manufacture a contribution where there is none.

Trim-pass cost is now the binding constraint, not draft quality. genesis 27 spans of 5330/3930/6923/7996/6875 gave entries of 646/649/648/647/649 - fifth clean chapter running, zero lint defects - but EVERY entry needed 3-6 trim passes, and the first drafts came in at 789/769/781/749/787 against a 650 ceiling. I set out to draft at 570-600 and consistently landed near 780. That is a systematic 30 percent overshoot, not noise. Recommendation for the loop doc: draft to a hard sentence budget rather than a word target - roughly 4 paragraphs of 4-5 sentences - since word-count intent alone does not control length.

Re-scrape (owner chose option c) is BLOCKED in this environment: the egress proxy denies www.studylight.org (403 at CONNECT) and WebFetch returns EGRESS_BLOCKED, so no source can be re-fetched from a CCR container. Workers have been rediscovering these one chapter at a time and excluding them by hand (exodus 29, exodus 40, numbers 4, numbers 10, numbers 26, joshua 15 all in the last day).

THE SENTENCE BUDGET FIXED THE OVERSHOOT. Last chapter I recorded a systematic 30 percent overshoot: five first drafts at 749-789 words against a 650 ceiling, after explicitly aiming at 570-600. This chapter I drafted to a hard STRUCTURAL budget instead - four paragraphs of four to five sentences - and four of the five entries landed inside the window on the FIRST pass (577, 626, 638, 622); only one needed trimming (732 to 650, and that one had run to five long sentences per paragraph). Total trim passes for the chapter: 6, against roughly 25 last time. Recommendation for docs/agents/cow-synthesis-loop.md: state the drafting target as a sentence count and paragraph count, not a word count. A word target does not control length; a sentence count does.

NO JFB BLOCKS AT ALL in leviticus 16 - the first chapter in this whole series with none, so no scrape residue to check or exclude. Worth knowing that the JFB gap is not uniform: where JFB is absent the residue problem simply does not arise, and a repair sweep can skip such chapters entirely. Someone should count how many chapters lack JFB blocks; if the absence correlates with book or section it may indicate which part of the scrape failed.

Two cross-span dependencies in this chapter that a per-span writer could easily miss. (1) The Sadducee dispute over where the incense was kindled (Gill, v13) and the oath sworn to the high priest on the eve (Ellicott, v17) are the same controversy reported by two commentators eleven verses apart; they belong together and I linked them across entries 5-14 and 15-19. (2) The meaning of Azazel is argued by Clarke at v10 (goat + dismiss, so simply the goat sent away) and settled flatly the other way by Gill at v26 ('the goat and Azazel are different, not the same, nor to be confounded as they are in our version'), sixteen verses later - so Gill lines up with Ellicott's proper-name reading against Clarke. A writer working strictly span by span would report the v10 debate as unresolved.

Ellicott is unusually load-bearing here, supplying second-Temple practice that the text itself does not describe and sometimes contradicts: the goat is merely let go in the law but was decreed to be destroyed at a rock twelve miles out with ten booths along the road; the written order of vv23-24 was reversed in practice; the hereditary high priesthood was treated as conditional on the elders judging the heir fit; and only sins against God were reckoned covered, wrongs to a neighbour needing his pardon first. Where a chapter is heavy with ritual, Ellicott carries more of the entry than the four-school balance suggests, and the grammatical-historical summary runs long as a result.

The Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block at psalms 100:3 is stride-6 residue of the kind now diagnosed corpus-wide: it carries Job 5:13 material (Paul quoting the clause in 1 Corinthians 3:19, Haman hanged on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai), nothing to do with knowing that the Lord is God. Declared in excluded_voices for entry 3, alongside Keil at v5 which is a bare Scripture quotation. StudyLight site chrome also trails Ellicott at v3.

THE OVERSHOOT IS FIXABLE, and the fix is sentence length rather than word budget. Prior workers logged a systematic ~30 percent overshoot on first drafts (see the genesis 27 note) and recommended drafting to a sentence budget; I tried that on psalms 133 last batch and still overshot, landing 710 and 720 against a 650 ceiling and needing five trim passes. This batch I changed something narrower: I wrote deliberately SHORTER SENTENCES — fewer subordinate clauses, one idea per sentence, semicolon chains broken into separate sentences — while keeping the same four-paragraph shape and the same amount of material. Both entries landed first time at 594 and 570 QA words, grade A, zero trim passes. The overshoot was never coming from paragraph count or from intending too much content; it came from clause accumulation inside sentences, which is invisible while drafting because each clause feels like a small addition. Recommendation for the loop doc: instruct the writer to cap sentences at roughly one subordinate clause and to break semicolon chains, rather than to target a word or sentence count.

JFB residue, seventeenth chapter: all three blocks are Genesis 15 material (the 'exceeding great reward' and the covenant rite with the lamp passing between the pieces). Keys 23 and 29 are byte-identical, the twofold duplication now seen in judges 1 and genesis 27 (where it was fourfold). Running donor list is now Gen 15, Gen 24, Gen 26, Gen 36, Gen 37, Lev 11, Lev 26, Deut 4, Deut 16-17, Deut 20-21, Deut 28, Exod 8-9 - overwhelmingly Pentateuch, and several of those donor chapters are themselves victims elsewhere. The displacement looks like a within-Pentateuch shuffle rather than a fixed offset.

SENTENCE BUDGET, SECOND TRIAL - holds, but only if sentence LENGTH is held too. Entries 9-15 (585) and 16-22 (615) landed in window first pass; entries 1-8 (766) and 23-33 (690) did not, and in both cases the cause was identifiable: I had let paragraphs run to five sentences AND let those sentences run long, several over 45 words. The rule that actually works is four paragraphs of four sentences with sentences kept near 35 words; adding a fifth sentence per paragraph adds roughly 150 words and blows the ceiling on its own. Trim passes this chapter: 3, against 6 last chapter and about 25 two chapters ago.

Two clean grammarian disagreements worth preserving as examples of the kind of debate the tags field exists for. (1) At v19 Ellicott concedes most versions favour the received rendering of 'for I know him', which makes Abraham's conduct earn the divine condescension, but argues the Hebrew means 'I have known him IN ORDER THAT he may command his sons' - shifting the ground from merit to purpose of calling. (2) At v21 Keil and Delitzsch take the disputed word as a NOUN on the evidence of Isaiah 10:23, which turns the clause into a sentence of utter destruction; Ellicott reports that reading, objects that its required ellipse is harsh, and keeps the adverb because inquiry rather than punishment is the prominent thought. Both are cases where two grammatical-historical voices divide against each other, which the single school summary cannot show - only the debates field can.

K&D block at v10 is bare verse quotation whose only comment ('After this conversation with Sarah, the heavenly guests rose up...') belongs to the NEXT span, so K&D had to be excluded from entry 9-15 even though the block sits inside it. This is the inverse of the genesis 27 case where a buried comment made an apparently bare block usable. Refined rule: read the tail of a quotation block before excluding, but check whether that tail comments on verses inside the span or merely transitions out of it - a transition sentence belongs to the following entry and cannot source the current one.

JFB stride-6 scrape residue confirmed in a repair-queue chapter. The only two JFB blocks in leviticus 15 are at v4 (tabernacle hooks and pillars, hanging up the carcasses of the sacrificial beasts) and v22 (the half-shekel census arithmetic, 603,550 men at 2s.4d. each). Neither has anything to do with beds or with a woman's separation. Both declared in excluded_voices; the ghost check flagged them unprompted.
Keil and Delitzsch at v33 is the bare verse text with no commentary attached, the tail of the concluding-formula block filed at v29. Declared in excluded_voices for the 31-33 entry rather than cited.

Sentence-length finding (note 320) holds on a chapter more than twice the size of psalms 100. Five entries, 12,383 usable source words: four landed in range on the first draft (637, 581, 482, 450) and only the 19-24 entry needed trimming, from 767. The one that overshot was the one whose material was a list — Ellicott's catalogue of ancient superstitions — where the short-sentence rule does not bite because each item is already its own clause. Where the material is argument rather than enumeration, one idea per sentence keeps the draft inside 650 without a trim pass.

Filing: Henry's only two blocks in the chapter are at v1 and v19, and the v19 block is a whole-chapter overview running through vv.25-31. Filed at v19, so it had to be spent in the 19-24 entry; the 25-30 and 31-33 entries carry no puritan-evangelical school as a result. Keil's concluding-formula note on v32's wider phrase is likewise filed at v29 and was left unused rather than dragged into an entry that does not contain v32.

Three live disputes recorded in the tags. v2: Ellicott takes 'flesh' as a euphemism for the private parts, Keil denies it from v13's 'bathe his flesh in water'. v18: Keil says the emission and not the act is unclean, Ellicott says the act pollutes both parties even in lawful marriage, Wesley refuses the reading outright as contrary to the whole current of scripture, the practice of the Jews, and the light of nature and reason. v19: Keil grounds the seven days in the significance of the number seven, Ellicott in the need to cover exceptional cases as after childbirth.

JFB stride-6 residue again, and this chapter shows the stride cleanly: the only three JFB blocks in genesis 46 sit at vv.5, 11 and 29, six apart, and all three are Genesis 39-40 material (Potiphar's wife's remonstrance, her accusation of Joseph, Joseph interpreting the butler's and baker's dreams). None has anything to do with the descent into Egypt. Declared in excluded_voices for the three entries that contain them.

Keil and Delitzsch at v9 and v33 are bare verse text with no exposition attached — the tails of blocks whose commentary is filed at v6 and v32. Declared in excluded_voices for the 8-27 and 33-34 entries rather than cited.

Calvin at v8 rejects a solution of the seventy/seventy-five discrepancy that he attributes to Augustine. The ghost check flags Augustine as a cited voice absent from the span, which is a false positive: he is named inside Calvin's own text, not as a commentary voice, and the corpus fidelity check grounds the attribution. He is correctly absent from the entry's voices list, so no badge is affected. Kept the name because dropping it would misreport whose argument Calvin was answering.

Filing rule caught a live error during drafting. Keil's note on the closing formula, 'all the souls of the house of Jacob', is filed at v6 — inside the 1-7 span — and I had cited it in the 8-27 entry where it reads more naturally. Removed. Keil has no real commentary anywhere in 8-27 (v9 is bare verse text), so the correct outcome was excluded_voices, not a borrowed citation. Worth noting that the natural reading order and the filing order diverge most where a commentator's block runs past the verse it is filed under.

JFB scrape residue, eighteenth chapter found: all six Jamieson blocks in numbers 35 are Numbers 11-12 material (Moses' remonstrance, the seventy elders, the quails, Eldad and Medad, the Cushite woman). Notable as a clear WITHIN-BOOK displacement -- every prior donor identified was a different book. Running donor list: Gen 15, 24, 26, 36, 37; Lev 11, 26; Deut 4, 16-17, 20-21, 28; Exod 8-9; now Num 11-12. Excluded via RESIDUE at every key.

Block-keying loss: Henry keys his ENTIRE chapter exposition at v9 -- both the law of murder/manslaughter (vv16-33) and the gospel typology of the refuge cities. He is therefore unavailable to entry 22-34, which has no puritan-evangelical voice at all. Declared rather than distorting the tiling: pulling 22-34 back into the 9-21 entry would have made a 21-verse block of 11,226 source words, unwritable inside the 650-word ceiling. Chose three entries (1-8 / 9-21 / 22-34) over four so that Henry covers two of three rather than two of four.

The 1,000-vs-2,000-cubit discrepancy between vv4 and 5 draws FIVE rival solutions across the corpus -- unusually many. Calvin: v5 merely explains how v4 is measured, and doubling is a subterfuge (geometrical circuit reading). Wesley: v4 gives the space FROM which to measure, v5 the space TO which, totalling three thousand. Gill with Jarchi and the Mishnah: 1,000 inner for suburbs plus 2,000 outer for fields and vineyards. Clarke: notes LXX and Coptic read 2,000 in both verses but concedes no MS collated by Kennicott and De Rossi supports it, so falls back on Maimonides. Ellicott adds Michaelis, who would add the length of the city wall so suburbs scale with the town.

Calvin dissents from the plain sense of the avenger-of-blood licence (v19), calling private vengeance a savour of barbarism and a very bad precedent, and reads the text as denouncing a danger rather than opening a gate -- tolerated, not approved, conceded to hardness of heart. Gill reaches the same restraint by citing the Targum of Jonathan and Onkelos ('in judgment', i.e. once the court has condemned). Henry, by contrast, accepts the next-of-kin execution as the natural counterpart of the kinsman-redeemer, limited only by the requirement of notorious evidence.

DROPPED, needs an owner decision (same class as numbers 31). nehemiah 7 is a repair pick whose existing entries are 50 percent UNSOURCED by the audit -- e.g. key 12 attributes detailed claims about the number of the children of Elam to Keil, Ellicott, Clarke, Gill, Wesley and Henry, when the only block at key 12 is JFB scrape residue (1 Chronicles 3, David's sons) and Ellicott has no block anywhere in this chapter's catena. The repair cannot be written under the current rules. The catena has only 22 keys for 73 verses (1-8, 12, 19, 24, 33-34, 48, 54, 60, 68-73), and coverage_problems forbids a declared range from covering a verse absent from the source, so pericopes cannot bridge the gaps: the tiling is forced to nine runs. Four of those runs (12, 24, 48, 60) are PURE JFB residue with zero usable source, and three more (19 at 24w, 33-34 at 65w, 54 at 30w) fall far below the 120-word thin floor. There is no cow-sources/ per-commentator file for nehemiah 7 to draw on. Options for the owner: (a) allow a declared range to bridge source-key gaps when the gap verses have no catena at all, which would permit 1-8 / 9-67 / 68-73 and make the chapter writable; (b) allow deletion of residue-only keys; (c) re-scrape. A drafted two-entry version (1-4 and 5-73, 486w and 596w, all five real voices, both passing lint and the fidelity audit at 0 percent unsourced) was discarded solely because of the tiling rule.

Cleanest stride-6 JFB case in the corpus so far. Leviticus 19 has exactly five JFB blocks and they sit at vv.7, 13 apart from nothing else — 7, 19, 25, 31, 37, six apart with no exceptions. Every one is Exodus 40 or Leviticus 1-2 material: the cloud filling the tabernacle at v7, the laying on of hands at v19, the inward purity of the offerer at v25, the turtledoves for the poor at v31, the meat offering at v37. None touches the holiness code. All five declared in excluded_voices; the ghost check flagged exactly those five and nothing else across eleven entries.

Span planning had to be revised three times mid-chapter, and the revisions were the reason the chapter landed. Leviticus 19 is 39,867 usable source words over 37 contiguous keys with a median of 901 — sixteen keys over 1,000 words. The first plan of 7 entries produced drafts at 885, 898 and 773 words against a 650 ceiling; no amount of trimming saves a draft that far over without gutting it. Splitting 15-18 into 15-16 and 17-18, 19-25 into 19-22 and 23-25, and 26-28 into 26-27 and 28 alone brought every entry into range, at 11 entries. The rule this suggests: when a span's source words exceed roughly 4,500, plan to split it before drafting rather than after, because the trim pass cannot recover a 200-word overshoot without dropping whole voices.

Eight live disputes recorded in the tags, an unusually dense chapter for them. v3: whether the sabbath is joined to the fifth commandment to limit filial obedience (Ellicott, Wesley) or to charge parents with the honour of the day (Henry). v14: whether the stumbling-block before the blind is literal (Clarke, Calvin) or figurative of misleading the ignorant (Ellicott, Henry). v16: whether standing against a neighbour's blood is a duty of rescue (Ellicott) or a prohibition of false witness (Clarke, Wesley). v18: whether self-love is the rule measuring love of neighbour, which Calvin denies against the schools. v19: three accounts of the mingled kinds — a creation distinction, prudential husbandry, a barrier against the nations. v23: whether the uncircumcised fruit is husbandry (Clarke, Ellicott) or a symbol under the first commandment (Calvin). v26: three readings of eating with the blood. v35: how the promise attached to just weights is to be taken.

SCRAPE OVERRUN, a defect distinct from the JFB residue and the first of its kind logged. The Calvin block at key 32 contains his genuine two-hundred-word comment on Joseph's bones and then runs on into the ENTIRE 'Translation of Calvin's Version of the Book of Joshua', chapters 1 through 7 and beyond -- roughly 4,600 words of unrelated text. The Ellicott block at key 33 ends with StudyLight page chrome: navigation, copyright notice, terms-of-use links and several hundred words of raw CSS. Consequence for budgeting: 'synthesis-loop.py size' reported joshua 24 at 28,838 usable source words and keys 32 and 33 at 5,155 and 3,971, but the real usable content of those two keys is about 3,650 combined. Spans planned off the reported figures will be mis-sized. This did NOT need excluded_voices, since Calvin's own comment at 32 is real and was used; the overrun is simply ignored. Suggests usable_source_words should learn to cut at the 'END OF THE COMMENTARY' marker and at the StudyLight footer.

JFB scrape residue, twentieth chapter found: all three Jamieson blocks in joshua 24 are Deuteronomy 18-19 material (the prophet like unto Moses, the rule requiring more than a single witness, the punishment of perjury). Second non-Pentateuch victim after nehemiah 7, so the pattern is no longer confined to the Pentateuch on either side. Running donor list: Gen 15, 24, 26, 36, 37; Lev 11, 26; Deut 4, 16-17, 18-19, 20-21, 28; Exod 8-9; Num 11-12; 1 Chr 3-4.

Block-keying: Henry files only three blocks in joshua 24, at keys 1, 15 and 29, and each is a running exposition covering the material well beyond its key -- the block at 1 covers vv1-14, the block at 15 covers vv14-24, the block at 29 covers vv29-33. Tiling was set from those three anchors, so entries 1-13, 14-18 and 29-31 carry Henry and entries 19-24, 25-28 and 32-33 have no puritan-evangelical voice. Also excluded Keil and Delitzsch from entry 32-33 under the bare-block rule: their block at key 32 is the verse text of 32 and 33 quoted with no comment attached.

Three substantive disputes in this chapter. (1) Where the assembly stood 'before God': Clarke states the difficulty at its sharpest, since the tabernacle was at Shiloh, canvasses the Septuagint reading of Shiloh, Shuckford and Mede, and settles it by the ark's portability; Calvin and Henry independently agree the ark was brought to Shechem; but Keil and Delitzsch expressly refuse to let 'the sanctuary of the LORD' at v26 mean the ark brought over for the ceremony. (2) 'Ye cannot serve the LORD': Clarke reports and rejects an emendation reading 'ye shall not cease to serve', ingenious but unsupported by any Kennicott or De Rossi manuscript; Wesley calls it moral not absolute impossibility; Calvin calls it an obtestation aimed at their obstinacy; Ellicott alone grounds it in Israel's actual practice of serving Jehovah alongside other national gods. (3) The strange gods to be put away: Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin read them as idols of the heart, Wesley and Ellicott as real images still kept, Ellicott adding that no images are ever recorded as buried or burned in obedience.

A rare explicit, named disagreement between two corpus voices. At v32 Keil and Delitzsch reject Calvin's reading of 'a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof' by name: 'Their meaning certainly was not that the wretched inhabitants were worn out by the laborious task of cultivating it, or that the land was pestilential... as Calvin maintains.' Keil reads it instead as the land being an apple of discord whose people waste away in the strife of the nations contending for so fruitful and well-placed a country. Ellicott independently lists all three candidate senses — scarcity, unhealthiness, strife — and inclines to Keil's. Wesley takes the unhealthiness reading and grounds it in the funerals the spies would have passed on their travels. Four positions, one of them a direct citation of another commentator by name; recorded in the tags debate for entry 32.

JFB stride-6 residue, third consecutive chapter to show it cleanly. Numbers 13 has exactly three JFB blocks, at vv.19, 25 and 31 — six apart — and all three are Exodus 12 / Leviticus 23 festival material (the passover as a perpetual memorial, the wave-sheaf of the barley firstfruits, the day after the passover sabbath). None touches the sending of the spies. All three declared in excluded_voices; the ghost check flagged those three and nothing else across eight entries.

The 4,500-word split rule from note 340 held on its first test, and is now better calibrated. Planned numbers 13 as 5 entries by pericope; three of the five drafted over the ceiling (854, 795, 709) and every one of them was a span above 4,000 source words, while both spans under 2,000 landed first time. Splitting to 8 entries fixed all three. But the rule needs a second clause: split on FILING, not just on size. Splitting 1-16 at v3 was forced by Calvin, whose entire contribution to the first sixteen verses — the choice of the tribes, the roll as a monument of ignominy, and the naming of Joshua — sits in one block filed at v2, so it had to travel with the 1-3 entry and could not follow the material it discusses into 4-16. The same constraint moved Henry's cluster-of-Eshcol reflection out of the 23-25 entry into 21-22, and Keil's grape-size note with it. Check where a commentator's block is filed before choosing the split point, or the split will strand material that cannot legally follow it.

Henry and Wesley read the same geography to opposite ends at vv.28-29, which made a clean debate for the tags. Wesley takes the list of nations as a catalogue of obstacles arranged by compass point — Amalek holding the southern entrance, the hill country in the south-east, the Canaanites guarding the east along the salt sea. Henry takes the identical dispersion as the spies' refutation: scattered as they were, the Canaanites could neither soon get together nor long keep together, so the report was cowardice and not intelligence. Henry adds the line the entry closes on, that the giants' overgrown stature would only make them the better mark, and the bulkiest men have not always the best mettle.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-first chapter found: all five Jamieson blocks in numbers 11 are Leviticus 21-22 material (priestly marriage restrictions, the high priest barred from mourning, physical defects disqualifying from service, purification by immersion). Two things are notable. First, keys 18 and 24 carry the IDENTICAL 105-word block, another instance of one residue block duplicated across keys (twofold in judges 1, genesis 18 and now here; fourfold in genesis 27). Second, numbers 11 is simultaneously DONOR and VICTIM: the six JFB blocks in numbers 35 were all Numbers 11-12 material, while numbers 11's own JFB blocks come from Leviticus 21-22. Running donor list: Gen 15, 24, 26, 36, 37; Lev 11, 21-22, 26; Deut 4, 16-17, 18-19, 20-21, 28; Exod 8-9; Num 11-12; 1 Chr 3-4.

SCRAPE OVERRUN confirmed a second time, so it is not a one-off. As in joshua 24, the Ellicott block at the LAST key of the chapter (here key 34) ends with StudyLight page chrome: navigation, copyright notice, terms-of-use links and several hundred words of raw CSS. joshua 24 also had the Calvin block at key 32 running on into the entire translation of Calvin's Joshua. The shared shape is that the overrun attaches to a block near the END of a chapter, which is where a scraper would run past the article body into the page footer. Consequence unchanged: 'synthesis-loop.py size' overstates the usable words of late keys, so spans planned off the reported figures are mis-sized. usable_source_words should learn to cut at the StudyLight footer marker (the run of 'terms of use / privacy policy / rights and permissions' links, or the first CSS selector) and at 'END OF THE COMMENTARY'.

Unusually clean block-keying: Henry files exactly six blocks in numbers 11, at keys 1, 4, 10, 16, 24 and 31, and those six anchors coincide exactly with the chapter's natural pericopes (Taberah; the mixed multitude and the manna; Moses' remonstrance; the seventy and the quails promised; the seventy prophesy with Eldad and Medad; the quails and the plague). Every entry therefore carries a puritan-evangelical voice, which has not happened in the last several chapters. One nuance: Henry's substantive treatment of Moses' remonstrance sits in the block at key 4, but he files a condensed version of the same material at key 10, so entry 10-15 is grounded independently. Calvin's block at key 30 is likewise mostly about the quails of vv31-32; that material was left unused rather than moved, since Calvin is independently present at keys 33 and 34.

Four substantive disputes. (1) v1, what the people complained of: nobody knows, and the sources fill the silence differently -- Gill cites Jarchi for men seeking a pretext to break with God, Clarke reports Jerome's conjecture of the length of the way, Wesley the three days of howling wilderness, Keil and Delitzsch decline to name a cause. Calvin makes it a grammatical question, listing four renderings of the participle (murmuring, being sick, dealing treacherously, seeking occasion) and rejecting all in favour of FAINTING, that they failed as men broken down with weariness. (2) v25, whether the seventy kept the gift: Wesley holds the Spirit took up a settled abode with them because the use of the gift was perpetual, Calvin that it was strictly temporary and served only as credentials, as prophecy did for Saul -- and the two read the SAME closing clause in opposite senses, Wesley 'they did not cease', Calvin and Ellicott 'they did so no more'. (3) v31, the two cubits: Clarke says the Hebrew will not bear a carpet of quails two feet thick and has them flying within reach of a club, following the Vulgate; Ellicott lays out both readings and grants the heap is the more obvious sense while objecting that heaped birds would need miraculous preserving since Israel might not eat what died of itself; Wesley takes a middle course of scattered heaps often two cubits high. (4) v33, the cause of the plague: Keil and Delitzsch expressly reject the toxic-quail theory (Knobel citing Bochart) for an extraordinary judgment, where Ellicott holds that such a surfeit would naturally produce much sickness and that the natural and supernatural are here combined; Clarke refuses to specify what the writer left unspecified.

Unusual source form: Clarke's blocks at keys 27, 28 and 29 are not prose commentary but three of Charles Wesley's hymns on this passage, quoted in full from 'Short Hymns on Select Passages of the Holy Scriptures' (Bristol, 1762), with Clarke's own closing remark that such sentiments are the more remarkable coming from a man otherwise sufficiently bigoted to ecclesiastical orders and regularity. Handled by reporting that Clarke answers the Eldad and Medad episode with poetry rather than comment, and attributing the hymns to Charles Wesley rather than to Clarke. Worth watching for elsewhere in Clarke: verse quoted as commentary is easy to mis-attribute to the commentator.

JFB stride-6 residue at its longest run yet: seven blocks in one chapter, at vv.2, 8, 20, 26, 32, 38 and 44 — six apart with no exceptions across a 48-verse chapter. Every one is Joshua 1-4 material (the pledge to Rahab, the caves of Quarantania, the instructions before crossing, the ark standing in Jordan, the twelve stones, the height of the river in harvest). Not one touches the war with Benjamin. All seven declared in excluded_voices; the ghost check flagged exactly those seven and nothing else across nine entries. Four consecutive chapters have now confirmed the stride.

Four live disputes recorded in the tags, two of them methodological rather than exegetical. v1 and v18: whether the oracle was consulted at Mizpeh and Bethel or at Shiloh — Keil and Ellicott hold Bethel, the ark having been fetched because Shiloh lay too far from the war, while Clarke and Gill hold that a deputation went to Shiloh where Phinehas was; Ellicott notes the English rendering 'house of God' has hidden Bethel from readers throughout the chapter. v35: why the narrative gives the result before the details — Keil defends the text against critics who called the summary spurious or took the following verses for a rival account, holding they have missed a habit of Hebrew historical writing; Ellicott accepts the same order but explains it by compilation from sources, one of which he thinks was a poem, or by a style he says a Roman would have called inconditus. v48: whether the extermination can be defended, where Ellicott weighs a good side (horror of moral pollution) against an evil one (ruthless savagery) and Clarke allows no good side at all.

Chapter with no Calvin and no Wesley anywhere in its source — the voice set is Gill, Ellicott, Keil, Clarke, Henry and JFB residue only. That collapses the school coverage: reformed is carried by Gill alone in every entry, wesleyan-arminian by Clarke alone, and puritan-evangelical appears only in the four entries containing Henry's blocks (vv.1, 12, 18, 26). Worth noting for anyone auditing school balance across the corpus: a thin school here is a property of the source, not of the synthesis. Henry's four blocks each run far past the verse they are filed under — the v26 block covers the rest of the chapter — so his material had to be spent in those four entries and the last three entries carry no puritan-evangelical voice at all.

SCRAPE OVERRUN, third confirmation and a NEW form. In joshua 24 and numbers 11 the overrun was CSS; here the Ellicott block at key 33 is 1,030 words of which only about 40 are real commentary, the remainder being the StudyLight footer followed by minified JAVASCRIPT (an accordion-navigation routine). Gill's block at the same key also ends with StudyLight breadcrumbs ('Next: Leviticus Chapter 23 Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous: John Gill's Exposition...'). The invariant across all three chapters is POSITION, not content type: the overrun attaches to blocks at the LAST key of the chapter, which is where a scraper runs past the article body into the page footer, and the junk may be CSS, JS, nav breadcrumbs, or another work entirely. A robust fix cuts at the footer marker -- the run of 'terms of use / privacy policy / rights and permissions' links, or the first CSS selector, or the first '(function(' -- and at 'END OF THE COMMENTARY'. Effect on budgeting: 'size' reported entry 26-33 at 3,781 words where the real usable figure is about 2,770, a 27 percent overstatement concentrated in one key.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-second chapter found: all four Jamieson blocks in leviticus 22 are Leviticus 4 material (the sin offerings for the congregation, for a ruler, and for a common person). Keys 6 and 12 carry the IDENTICAL 172-word block, the third chapter running with a duplicated residue block. Two further points. This is a WITHIN-BOOK displacement, Leviticus 4 into Leviticus 22. And leviticus 22 is itself the DONOR for numbers 11, whose five JFB blocks were all Leviticus 21-22 material -- so the chapter is donor and victim at once, the same pattern numbers 11 showed. Running donor list: Gen 15, 24, 26, 36, 37; Lev 4, 11, 21-22, 26; Deut 4, 16-17, 18-19, 20-21, 28; Exod 8-9; Num 11-12; 1 Chr 3-4.

Block-keying: Henry files three blocks in leviticus 22, at keys 1, 10 and 17, and the block at 17 is a running exposition of FOUR laws covering vv17-30 -- the unblemished victim, the eighth day, the dam and her young, and the thank-offering. Tiling was set from those three anchors, so entry 26-33 has no puritan-evangelical voice even though Henry discusses most of its material. Declared rather than distorting the tiling: folding 26-33 back into 17-25 would have made a 17-verse entry of roughly 9,000 source words, unwritable inside the 650-word ceiling.

Four substantive disputes. (1) v19, 'at your own will': Calvin denies the rendering outright, holding the Hebrew can only point to God's good pleasure, then concedes the other sense may stand if taken of gratuitous favour; Ellicott and Gill reach Calvin's result by translation alone ('that it may be accepted for you'). (2) v23, the freewill concession: the plain sense allows a disproportioned animal for a freewill offering but not for a vow, and Henry, Calvin and Clarke all work within it. Ellicott alone refuses it, arguing the lawgiver cannot contradict vv18-20 within three verses, that the second Temple read the verse as consecration for repairs rather than sacrifice, and that THE TEXT IS PROBABLY DISARRANGED and originally forbade the freewill offering too -- a conjectural emendation, not a gloss. (3) v25, the stranger's hand: Jewish canonists take the verse to regulate Gentile offerings; Calvin and Ellicott independently reject this, Calvin because the closing words say the sacrifice would not be accepted from Jews themselves, Ellicott because of the contrast between 'in your land' and 'from the hand of a foreigner'. (4) v27, why the eighth day: Keil and Delitzsch give the week sanctified by creation; Calvin explicitly names and dismisses that reason as TOO SUBTLE, objecting that on that ground the seventh day would be fittest, and rests on maturity alone, as with circumcision.

Three places where a commentator breaks frame, worth flagging as recurring Clarke and Ellicott habits. (1) Clarke at v27 attacks the Authorised Version itself -- 'a most unfortunate as well as absurd translation', since an ox is a bull castrated and so 'a bullock was never yet brought forth' -- and says only his rule of printing the common version with scrupulous exactness stops him from entering 'calf' into the text. He objects again at v32 to 'children of Israel', which he would render posterity. (2) Ellicott at v31 complains that rendering the conjunctions as 'therefore' and 'neither' mars the simple and dignified style of the original. (3) Ellicott at v24 notes the prohibition of gelding still binds orthodox Jews and that their teachers had lately been debating it because it bears hard on those of their community who farm -- a live nineteenth-century application, not an antiquarian note. Clarke does the same at v10, using the bought slave's standing in the priestly family to attack European Christians who cite the Mosaic law to justify slavery.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-third chapter found, and the most systematic duplication yet. All six Jamieson slots in numbers 21 are Numbers 1-2 material (the census and the order of encampment), but they are filled from only TWO distinct blocks: an 88-word block at keys 4 and 10, and a 137-word block at keys 16, 22, 28 and 34. Previous maximum was fourfold duplication in genesis 27; here one block is duplicated twice and another four times, so six slots carry two texts. THE NEW AND DIAGNOSTIC POINT: the affected keys are 4, 10, 16, 22, 28, 34 -- a perfect arithmetic stride of 6. That is not content-matching gone wrong; it looks like the scraper filling every sixth key from a small buffer of previously-read blocks, which would explain both the duplication and the regular spacing. Worth checking the other 22 residue chapters for the same stride. Within-book displacement again (Numbers 1-2 into Numbers 21). Running donor list: Gen 15, 24, 26, 36, 37; Lev 4, 11, 21-22, 26; Deut 4, 16-17, 18-19, 20-21, 28; Exod 8-9; Num 1-2, 11-12; 1 Chr 3-4.

Block-keying: Henry files four blocks in numbers 21, at keys 1, 4, 10 and 21, and each is a running exposition well beyond its key -- the block at 4 covers the whole serpent episode vv4-9 including the full typology, and the block at 21 covers vv21-30. Tiling was set from those anchors, so entries 26-31 and 32-35 have no puritan-evangelical voice. One deliberate choice worth recording: I considered splitting 4-9 into 4-5 and 6-9 to relieve a source-to-prose ratio of 11.6, and did not, because Henry's block sits at key 4 and the brazen-serpent typology is the richest material in the chapter; splitting would have handed the serpent to an entry that could not cite him. Compression was the better loss. Also note Clarke's block at key 35 is a long authorial APPENDIX (Kennicott's remarks on the whole chapter plus Lightfoot's note), not scrape overrun -- the same pattern as his Saurin outline at joshua 24:33. Genuine commentary appended at a chapter's end is easy to mistake for the footer defect; the test is whether it is prose about the text or page furniture.

Four substantive disputes, two of them flat contradictions. (1) v9, whether the brazen serpent is a type of Christ: Henry runs the parallel through disease, remedy and application; Wesley sets out shape, pole and looking; Ellicott and Calvin both read it as fulfilled in John 3:14. CLARKE DENIES IT OUTRIGHT -- 'the brazen serpent was certainly no type of Jesus Christ' -- calling a serpent the most exceptionable figure that could be chosen and objecting to running the parallel through ten or a dozen particulars, while still granting five parallels drawn from our Lord's own words. (2) v9 again, what the LIFTING UP figures: Calvin says it is 'poorly and incorrectly' explained as foreshadowing the crucifixion and belongs rather to the preaching of the gospel, his ground being that nes means a standard or mast set high to be seen from every side, answering Isaiah's ensign to the nations. Henry takes both without choosing. (3) v14, 'Vaheb in Suphah': Clarke calls it impenetrably obscure and says scarcely two commentators agree; he reports Calmet's emendation (adopted by Houbigant) that copyists' slips turned Zared into Vaheb, then proposes his own reading as a proverb of distance like 'from Dan even unto Beersheba'; Kennicott, whom Clarke prints at v35, places Suph near the meeting of Arnon and Jordan and reads the line as saying God brought Israel from the sea of Suph to Suph again; Calvin rejects the rendering 'book' that almost all translators give and takes Vaheb as a verb. (4) v29, where the Amorite ballad ends: Clarke divides it into three parts and Keil and Delitzsch into three strophes, both keeping vv29-30 inside the song; Wesley holds the Amorite song ends at v28 and the rest is Israel's own comment scoffing at Chemosh.

Two further habits worth tracking. (1) Clarke re-translating against the Authorised Version, now the third chapter running: at v18 he asks 'who can suppose that the princes dug this well with their staves?' and re-renders the song so that they SEARCHED IT OUT and digged it 'upon their own borders', reading chapharu as searched and bemishanotham as on their confines. Compare his 'a bullock was never yet brought forth' at leviticus 22:27. (2) Ellicott at vv25 and 31 argues that 'Israel dwelt in the cities of the Amorites' should be 'sojourned' or 'abode', of a temporary encampment, since the permanent settlement east of Jordan came only after Moses' death. Calvin reaches the same conclusion from theology rather than philology -- God had not yet declared them masters east of Jordan, and the cities were destroyed precisely so that a slothful people should find no comfortable resting-place short of Canaan. Independent agreement from opposite methods is worth noting where it occurs.

The sharpest head-to-head in the corpus so far: at v31 Ellicott rebuts, point by point and without naming him, every argument Clarke makes for the consecration reading of Jephthah's vow. Clarke: conditions must have been implied, or the vow would be a heathen's or a madman's; the man was pious and knew the law; a lost letter turned 'I will offer Him a burnt offering' into 'I will offer it up for a burnt offering'; and v39 shows the daughter consecrated to virginity. Ellicott: the rendering is whosoever not whatsoever, and the marginal 'or' for 'and' comes of the same wish to soften the verse, following Kimchi in explaining the plain sense away out of deference to modern feeling; the animal reading is a notion Augustine ridiculed and a strangely inadequate return besides; human sacrifice was the special worship of the very nations Jephthah was marching against. On the strongest of Clarke's points — that the Spirit of the Lord was on him — Ellicott answers that the Spirit clothed Gideon who set up an illegal worship, came on Saul who was ready to kill his own son over a vow, and came on David who sank into adultery and murder, the phrase being a grant of strength for a particular end and no certificate of attainment. The dispute recurs at v40 over whether the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament her or to praise her, which is the same question asked of the verb.

Second occurrence of the Augustine ghost-check false positive (first recorded at genesis 46:8, note 332). At v31 Ellicott writes that the animal reading of the vow is 'a notion which even St. Augustine ridicules'; I reported that, and the ghost check flagged Augustine as a cited voice absent from the span. As before this is a name occurring inside another commentator's prose, not a commentary voice: Augustine has no block anywhere in judges 11, he is correctly absent from the entry's voices list so no badge is affected, and the corpus fidelity audit grounds the attribution at 0 percent unsourced. The pattern is now established enough to be worth a rule: when the ghost check reports a single ghost that is a Church Father, check whether the name is being quoted by Ellicott or Calvin before treating it as a defect.

JFB stride-6 residue, fifth consecutive chapter. Seven blocks in judges 11, at vv.2, 8, 14, 20, 26, 32 and 38 — six apart with no exceptions — and every one is Deuteronomy 29-31 material (the whole congregation assembled to renew the Sinaitic covenant, the curses on a land whose people forsook it, the promise of restoration and the circumcised heart, the law that is not hidden in heaven). None touches Jephthah. All seven declared in excluded_voices. Judges 20 gave the same count in the same book from a Joshua 1-4 donor, so a single book can draw residue from more than one donor passage.

Second chapter running with no Calvin and no Wesley in the source (judges 20 was the first), so reformed rests on Gill alone and wesleyan-arminian on Clarke alone throughout. Henry has four blocks, at vv.1, 4, 12 and 29, and the span plan was built around them so that each landed in a distinct entry — otherwise the last four entries would have carried no puritan-evangelical voice at all rather than the two they do. Planning the splits against the filing map before drafting, rather than by source-word count alone, is what kept the school coverage even; it is the same lesson as note 348 and is now worth treating as standard procedure for any chapter where one voice supplies a school by itself.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-fourth chapter, and the stride hypothesis from numbers 21 is CONFIRMED IN A DIFFERENT BOOK and refined. The five Jamieson slots here sit at keys 5, 11, 17, 23, 29 -- a stride of exactly 6, as in numbers 21 (keys 4, 10, 16, 22, 28, 34). Two chapters in different books showing the same arithmetic spacing is no longer coincidence. The refinement is more diagnostic still: the blocks are Exodus 10-11 material laid down IN NARRATIVE ORDER -- key 5 the locusts (Ex 10:12ff), key 11 the same block repeated byte-for-byte, key 17 the darkness and Pharaoh's compromise (Ex 10:21ff), key 23 the seven-word fragment 'Moses said, Thou hast spoken well' (Ex 10:29), key 29 the announcement of the last plague (Ex 11:1ff). So the scraper is not drawing at random from a buffer: it walks the DONOR chapter sequentially while writing into every sixth key of the VICTIM, occasionally stalling and repeating the current block (keys 5 and 11 are md5-identical). This predicts that residue keys in other chapters will be arithmetic, that residue content will be in donor order, and that duplicates will be ADJACENT in the stride rather than scattered. Worth a sweep over the other 22 logged chapters to test all three. Within-book displacement again (Exodus 10-11 into Exodus 23).

METHODOLOGICAL WARNING, first time logged and it affects how the whole corpus should be read: in exodus 23 Wesley's notes are VERBATIM ABRIDGEMENTS OF HENRY, not independent comment. Compare v1 -- Henry: 'That which we translate, Thou shalt not raise, the margin reads, Thou shalt not receive a false report; for sometimes the receiver, in this case, is as bad as the thief; and a backbiting tongue would not do so much mischief as it does if it were not countenanced.' Wesley: 'Thou shalt not raise, the margin reads, Thou shalt not receive a false report, for sometimes the receiver in this case is as bad as the thief; and a backbiting tongue would not do so much mischief, if it were not countenanced.' The same holds at v2 (the 'too great a compliment, to be willing to go to hell for company' passage), at v13 (the paragraph on Christian schools and academies and the play-houses), and at v25 (bread and water against a feast of fat things). CONSEQUENCE: where Wesley and Henry agree, that is ONE witness and not two, and a school tally that counts puritan-evangelical and wesleyan-arminian separately overstates the breadth of agreement. Handled here by writing 'Henry, whom Wesley follows almost word for word' rather than presenting them as concurring independently. Worth checking how widely this holds; Wesley's Explanatory Notes are known to be heavily drawn from Henry and from Bengel, so the corpus may carry this throughout the Old Testament.

Four substantive disputes. (1) v5, the fallen ass: the verb is disputed and Jerome departed widest; Calvin canvasses the interrogative reading and rejects it for the imperative, concluding the law was framed to put enemies to work side by side over a suffering animal and so give them occasion for reconciliation; ELLICOTT ADOPTS A CONJECTURAL EMENDATION, Geddes' 'azar for 'azab in all three places the verb occurs. (2) v19, the kid in its mother's milk, four ways: Clarke reports Cudworth's Karaite manuscript on a heathen magical rite and Wesley repeats it; ELLICOTT CALLS THAT FANCIFUL and refutes it from Deuteronomy 14:21, where the precept stands among unclean meats and so concerns a kid boiled to be eaten, preferring Bochart on the cruelty of making the milk meant to feed it the means of cooking it; CALVIN REJECTS THE DIETARY READING ALTOGETHER, arguing from the threefold repetition and the company each occurrence keeps that the precept belongs to the sacrifices. (3) v20, who the Angel is: Gill collects the rabbinic options (the book of the law, the ark, Michael, Metatron); Kalisch says Moses and the rabbis Joshua; Henry gives created-angel and Son-of-God without deciding; Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin and Wesley all take the pre-incarnate Son, Calvin refuting Joshua on the ground that Israel would then have had no leader in the desert, and Ellicott offering the neatest argument, that God is never said to set his Name in a man. (4) v28, the hornets: Gill and Clarke literal (Aelian on the Phaselites; Clarke's own forceps anecdote; Joshua 24:12); Aben Ezra and the Arabic version a wasting disease; Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott not literal since Joshua records no such extermination, ELLICOTT PROPOSING THE EGYPTIANS, whose armies broke the Hittites while Israel was in the desert and whose hieroglyph for king was a bee.

Three places where a commentator reasons past the text, worth tracking. (1) Clarke at v11 observes that the keeping of the sabbatical year is NOWHERE EXPRESSLY RECORDED in Scripture, and infers that the people could not trust God that far until the captivity gave the land the sabbaths their unbelief had denied it -- an argument from silence, but a disciplined one, and he flags it as his own inference. (2) Calvin at v24 separates the permanent from the temporary inside a single command, holding that the condemnation of superstition stands to the end of the world while the order to demolish was an enactment for that time, and draws the contemporary consequence without hesitation: Christians may retain buildings once polluted by idols and put them to better use. He then follows Augustine in denying private individuals any commission to destroy idols, the authority belonging to a people once they hold the country -- a live sixteenth-century application. (3) Ellicott at v32 explains the otherwise puzzling clause 'nor with their gods' from the diplomacy of the period, since treaties between nations regularly acknowledged each other's deities, citing the treaty between Rameses II and the Hittites in the Records of the Past. That is the kind of external evidence the older commentators had no access to, and it resolves the clause cleanly.

New kind of excluded_voices case, and one the owner may want a ruling on. Clarke's entire block at exodus 34:28 is 'Forty days and forty nights - See Clarke's note on Exo 24:18' — a bare cross-reference with no exposition whatever. That is neither declared scrape residue nor a bare Scripture quotation, which are the two categories excluded_voices is documented for, yet synthesis_qa.undeclarable_voices judges it declarable and the ghost check auto-excluded it. I accepted the tool's judgement rather than cite a pointer as though it were commentary, but the rule as written in the loop doc does not cover contentless cross-references. Suggest either widening the documented categories to include them or leaving the case explicitly to worker judgement; either way it should be written down, since Clarke does this often.

The filing rule bit twice in one chapter, and the ghost check caught the second instance only because Henry happens to be absent from the span. Matthew Henry's block at v28 runs through v35, so his exposition of the shining face — the credentials carried in the countenance, and the comparison with the transfiguration where our Lord laid his glory aside — is filed at v28 and cannot travel into the 29-30 entry where it reads most naturally. I had drafted it there; the ghost check flagged Henry as a cited voice absent from the span and I moved the transfiguration comparison back into the v28 entry and reattributed the rest to Wesley, who says nearly the same thing in his own block at v29. Same thing happened at v5, where Henry's and Calvin's exposition of the divine attributes is filed at the verse that only says the Lord descended, while the attributes themselves are in vv.6-7. Where a commentator's block runs several verses past its filing point, the ghost check is the only thing standing between the filing rule and a silent violation.

Two clean disputes recorded in the tags. v1: who wrote the second tables. Ellicott says it is quite clear, though some have maintained the contrary, that they were inscribed by the finger of God as the first were, and Keil agrees the Hebrew idiom permits Jehovah as the subject of 'he wrote' at v28 and that Deuteronomy requires it; Clarke reaches the same result by a different route, distinguishing two documents — God engraving the tables laid up in the ark, Moses writing an authenticated copy for the congregation, which he says removes the apparent contradiction and lets both statements stand. v33: when the veil went on. Gill defends the Authorised rendering and explicitly rejects the Septuagint's 'when he had done', arguing that on that reading there would have been no occasion for a veil at all; Ellicott says the English exactly inverts the meaning and that the veil went on when the speaking was over, becoming part of Moses' ordinary dress and laid aside only before God and when delivering a message.

JFB stride-6 residue, sixth consecutive chapter, and the donor is Deuteronomy again. Four blocks in exodus 34, at vv.2, 8, 26 and 32, six apart, all Deuteronomy 15-30 material (the Hebrew slave freed in the seventh year and the brand on the ear, the redemption of Hebrew girls, the law of retaliation as a civil rule mistaken by later Jews for a moral precept, the promise of restoration from dispersion). None touches the renewal of the covenant. All four declared in excluded_voices.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-fifth chapter, and the stride-6 pattern holds in a THIRD book. The two Jamieson slots sit at keys 3 and 9 -- stride of 6, matching numbers 21 (4,10,16,22,28,34) and exodus 23 (5,11,17,23,29). Three books, three chapters, same arithmetic spacing. The content confirms the sequential-donor finding as well: both blocks are Genesis 18 material and they appear IN NARRATIVE ORDER, key 3 carrying the visitors approaching the chief sheik's tent (Gen 18:2) and key 9 carrying the women's apartment behind the partition (Gen 18:9-10). So the model established at exodus 23 stands: the scraper walks the donor chapter forward while writing into every sixth key of the victim. What differs here is scale -- only two slots, because genesis 21's donor run was short or the walk began late. Note also that the offset varies by chapter (first residue key is 3 here, 4 in numbers 21, 5 in exodus 23), so the stride is fixed at 6 but the phase is not. A mechanical sweep should therefore look for arithmetic sequences of period 6 at any offset, not for a fixed key set. Within-book displacement again (Genesis 18 into Genesis 21).

The Wesley-follows-Henry finding first logged at exodus 23 is CONFIRMED IN GENESIS and is clearly systematic rather than local. Verbatim or near-verbatim overlaps here at v2 ('Sarah by faith received strength to conceive... Abraham was old, and Sarah old, and both as good as dead, and then the word of God took place'), v4 ('The covenant being established with him, the seal of the covenant was administered to him'), v9 (the Egyptian and the four hundred years), v17 ('his sighs and groans cried loud in the ears of the God of mercy' and 'God's readiness to help us must not slacken but quicken our endeavours'), and v33 (the whole grove-and-oratory paragraph and the everlasting God). Two books now, twelve or more matched passages. CONSEQUENCE, restated because it matters for every chapter in the corpus: Wesley agreeing with Henry is one witness, not two, and any tally that counts puritan-evangelical and wesleyan-arminian as independent schools overstates agreement wherever Wesley is drawing on Henry. Handled here as at exodus 23, by writing 'Wesley, following Henry' or attributing the substance to Henry and noting Wesley's repetition. Where Wesley departs from Henry -- as he strikingly does at v13, see the disagreement note -- that is worth flagging precisely because it is his own.

Five substantive disputes. (1) v9, what the mocking was: Clarke reports the Targums' charge of an idolatrous rite and dismisses the whole question with 'conjectures are as useless as they are endless'; Ellicott brackets it between gross wickedness (rejected, since Abraham would not then have grieved) and the Septuagint's harmless playing (rejected, since Sarah's anger would then be unjust), and blames polygamy rather than either party; Calvin locates it in the shared root of the participle and the name Isaac, making both sons of laughter in opposite senses. (2) v10, 'bondwoman': ELLICOTT JUDGES THE AUTHORISED RENDERING MISLEADING, since ammah means handmaid and is used of a king's secondary wives, and holds that the English 'unduly depresses Hagar's condition, and with it that of the Jewish Church in the allegory'. Clarke independently softens the other term, arguing garash means to divorce as well as to expel. (3) v13, WESLEY BREAKS WITH THE SEVERITY OF THE REST: 'the casting out of Ishmael was not his ruin. We are not sure that it was his eternal ruin. It is presumption to say, that all these who are left out of the external dispensation of God's covenant are excluded from all his mercies.' This is the sharpest place in the chapter where Wesley is NOT following Henry, and it stands directly against Calvin's account of the two seeds. (4) v19, the well: Calvin, Clarke and Ellicott (with Abravanel) all hold it already existed and that Hagar's eyes were opened to see it; Gill allows that God may have created it on the spot and repeats the rabbinic notion that it was made at the world's beginning. (5) v33, 'called on the name of the LORD': CLARKE FOLLOWS SHUCKFORD IN CALLING THE AUTHORISED RENDERING 'VERY ERRONEOUS', since kara beshem means to invoke IN the name, not to call UPON the name, and takes it of prayer offered in the name of a mediator.

Three notable excursions. (1) Calvin at v12, before expounding Paul's allegory of the two sons, enters an explicit methodological caution: Paul's use is no warrant for torturing every history into allegory 'as Origen does, who by hunting everywhere for allegories corrupts the whole Scripture; and others, too eagerly emulating his example, have extracted smoke out of light'. He then turns the allegory polemically, that boasting of a long succession 'just means as much as if Ishmael were proclaiming himself the firstborn'. Worth noting as a commentator policing his own method before using it. (2) Ellicott at v22 makes a judgment against the patriarch that the other sources pass over: seeing Abraham now powerful enough for a king to seek alliance, he remarks that 'his abandonment of Sarah, and his receiving of presents in compensation for the wrong done her, seems the more unworthy of him', while Abimelech 'acts generously as of old'. (3) Clarke at v33 runs the chapter's longest excursion, from the Hebrew word for the tree through Romulus's asylum between two oak groves, the oracle at Dodona, the oak sacred to Jupiter, the Druids named from the oak, and Pliny on cutting the mistletoe with a golden hook -- ending in a christological reflection on one who had no father on earth and after being cut off was wrapped in fine linen. He then adds a philological argument on olam and aion with an explicitly polemical application to the duration of future punishment. Both Clarke habits, the antiquarian excursus and the doctrinal application of a word study, are now well attested across chapters.

JFB stride-6 residue streak breaks here. Six consecutive chapters (leviticus 15, genesis 46, leviticus 19, numbers 13, judges 20, judges 11, exodus 34) carried JFB blocks at a regular stride of 6 keys, each a run of donor text from a neighbouring book. genesis 11 has JFB at v26 ONLY -- a single isolated block, and its content is the Nimrod material of Genesis 10:8-10 (hunting wild beasts, founding the first kingdom), which has nothing to do with Terah begetting Abram. Declared as excluded_voices on the 10-26 entry; undeclarable_voices agreed. Worth watching whether the stride pattern resumes in the next chapters or whether isolated single-block residue is a second, distinct defect mode.

Span plan revised twice mid-chapter, both times before drafting the affected entry, and both revisions were right. (1) 2-4 split into 2-3 + 4: Wesley's material on the builders' two aims and his flood-refuge objection is filed at v3, so keeping v4 in the span would have stranded it. This is the filing rule of notes 348/376 applied to span CHOICE rather than to citation. (2) 6-9 split into 6-7 + 8-9 and 27-30 split into 27 + 28-30: both spans were under the ~4,500-word threshold of note 340 (4,266 and 3,703) but the material was dense enough that a single 650-word entry would have had to drop whole voices -- Clarke's Du Bartas and Wesley's Pentecost at 6-7, Ellicott's cuneiform account of Ur at 28. Sizing by source words alone is necessary but not sufficient; density of distinct arguments per word matters too. Ten entries, all grade A, none over 650.

Was Abram the firstborn of Terah? Henry, Calvin and Wesley say no, and Gill agrees: Terah died at 205 (v32), Abram left Haran at 75 after his father's death (Acts 7:4, Gen 12:4), so Abram was born in Terah's 130th year and is named first for dignity, not birth order. Calvin defends this at length, rejecting Luther's guess that God buried the sixty years in oblivion to hide the end of the world ('frivolous') and the alternative that Abram lived sixty years with Terah at Charran ('most improbable'). Ellicott alone holds the opposite: to deny Abram the birthright and give him first place for spiritual pre-eminence 'is contrary to the rules of the Hebrew language', and he appeals to the parallel failed attempt to strip Shem of his birthright by mistranslating Gen 10:21. Recorded as a debate on entry 27.

What the tower was for -- a genuine four-way split, recorded as a debate on entry 4. (a) A refuge against a second flood: reported by Gill, Clarke, Henry, Ellicott and Calvin, and rejected by every one of them. Calvin: those who conjecture it 'have no guide but the dream of their own brain'. Henry's objection is the practical one, that men with that in view would have built on a mountain, not a plain. (b) A temple to the host of heaven (Hutchinson, with 'one lip' read as one litany), or the Targums' talisman bearing an image with a sword: reported by Clarke without endorsement. (c) A beacon plus a centre of government to keep mankind from separating: Ellicott, who then doubts aloud whether centralisation promotes human happiness. (d) Nothing but ambition for an enduring name: Calvin, who hears behind it the fable of the giants heaping mountains to pull Jove from his throne.

JFB stride-6 residue confirmed here, and the isolated single block seen at genesis 11:26 (note 383) was the anomaly, not a new normal. joshua 13 carries JFB at v22 and v28 only -- exactly six keys apart -- and both blocks are the SAME sentence: 'After mentioning those instances of the divine goodness, Moses founded on them an argument for their future obedience.' That is Deuteronomy donor text, unrelated to Balaam's death or to the summary of Gad's inheritance. Two observations worth carrying forward: (1) the stride is 6 again after the genesis 11 break, so the defect is periodic in the scrape rather than content-driven; (2) a stride run can repeat one identical sentence at every stop rather than serialising a continuous donor passage, which is a cheaper signature to detect than the multi-block runs seen in judges 20 and judges 11. Both auto-declared by undeclarable_voices and filed as excluded_voices on entries 15 and 24.

Why Balaam's death is recorded in a land-allotment list. Ellicott makes it evidence: the verse calls the Midianite princes 'dukes of Sihon', which supplies a reason for the Midianite war beyond the one Numbers gives (that Midian tempted Israel to idolatry) -- they were part of Sihon's government, through whom he held the territory taken from Moab, so removing them completed the conquest. The relation between Midian and Moab is implied but never explained in Numbers, and Ellicott calls the casual remark here an undesigned agreement between Joshua and the Pentateuch; he reads the epithet 'soothsayer' the same way, since Numbers reports only prophecy from Balaam's lips yet the elders came with 'the reward of divination' in their hands. Clarke takes the flat opposite: both verses 'seem to be borrowed' from Numbers 31 and 'the introduction of the death of Balaam here seems quite irrelevant'. Recorded as a debate on entry 15.

Is the Sihor 'before Egypt' the Nile? Gill reports Jarchi and Kimchi for the Nile, named from its black and turbid waters (Greek Melas, Latin Melo), but doubts the river itself is meant since it does not reach the borders of Palestine, and settles for a branch. Calvin follows the received opinion for the Nile while explicitly refusing to repudiate the alternative of the stream past Rhinocorura. Keil and Delitzsch decide against the Nile on two grounds -- it is always called simply 'the river' in plain prose, and it flowed through the middle of Egypt rather than 'before' (east of) it -- and identify the Sichor with the brook of Egypt. Clarke prints a friend's opinion agreeing, on the ground that a wide desert lay between the river of Egypt and the isthmus of Suez and Solomon reigned to the borders of Egypt but not to the Nile. Recorded as a debate on entry 2; note that the modern consensus (Wadi el-Arish) is stated in the Calvin apparatus itself, in an editorial footnote rather than in Calvin's own text.

Sizing check for joshua 13. 16,048 usable source words, 33 contiguous keys, median 243, only vv.1 and 7 over 2k -- one of the smallest chapters offered by the picker in this run, and it took FIVE entries (1 | 2-6 | 7-14 | 15-23 | 24-33) rather than the seven a naive words-per-entry estimate suggests.
