Eight for eight on the terminal verse of a chapter is not a coincidence of harvesting but a boundary condition in the fetcher, and should be fixed there rather than stripped chapter by chapter.

Keil and Delitzsch appears in four blocks of this chapter that contain no commentary at all. At verses 2, 10, 17 and 23 the harvested block is the bare text of the verses that follow, sometimes running six or eight verses ahead and breaking off in mid-sentence, with the actual exposition attaching to a later key. The effect is that Keil is present by name in the source at verse 2 but has nothing whatever to say there, so the 1-2 entry had to exclude him — the only exclusion in this chapter not caused by donor residue. Where his exposition does exist it is filed one or two verses after the matter it treats (the Migdal Eder note under verse 17, the arrival at Mamre under verse 23), which forces material across span boundaries. This looks like a paragraph-splitting fault in the Keil harvest rather than a fault in the source text, and it is worth checking whether other Keil chapters carry the same empty leading blocks.

The trim burden recorded in note 557 did not improve and is now the dominant cost of a chapter. Across the thirteen entries of genesis 38 and genesis 35 the first draft averaged about 40 per cent over the 650-word ceiling, the worst single case being 1282 words for an entry that had to land at 635, and every entry needed between six and eleven trimming passes. The cause is visible in the source profile rather than in the writing: both chapters run five to seven voices at nearly every verse, and a span of three or four such verses offers twenty to thirty distinct items where the entry has room for ten or twelve. Drafting to a 700-word target does not help when the selection is made while writing rather than before it. What did work, in the later entries, was listing the items first and striking two-thirds of them before a sentence was written; what did not work was shaving clauses, which reliably returned five to nine words a pass. The discipline to carry forward is to fix the item list before drafting, and to treat any first draft over 800 words as a selection failure to be re-selected rather than trimmed.

Jamieson stride-6 confirmed for an ELEVENTH consecutive chapter. exodus 12 Jamieson keys: 8, 14, 20, 32, 38 - offset 2 mod 6, five members, gap at 26. Running table: joshua 10 (offset 1, 7 members, gap 31), 1corinthians 7 (5, 6, none), hebrews 11 (3, 5, gap 21), romans 8 (2, 7, none), romans 9 (4, 3, gaps 10/16), 1corinthians 15 (0, 7, gap 30), leviticus 27 (4, 6, none), judges 16 (3, 4, none), exodus 28 (1, 4, gaps 19/25/31), judges 19 (3, 5, none), exodus 12 (2, 5, gap 26). Offset 2 has now appeared twice (romans 8, exodus 12). The residue here is drawn from GENESIS, the preceding book: v8, v14 and v32 carry Joseph material (his mourning for Jacob, his forgiveness of his brothers, the embalming and Egyptian funeral), v20 is the Shoterim, and v38 is Egyptian brickmaking under Thothmes III. This is the second chapter after judges 19 where the residue crosses backward into the previous book, and it fits the same model: a single row pointer walking a canonical-order index at a fixed stride and lagging its target, so that an early chapter in a book draws residue from the end of the book before. Exodus 12 is early in Exodus and the residue sits at the end of Genesis, roughly a dozen chapters behind. Eleven chapters, seven books, every residue class mod 6 attested, both same-book and cross-book lag, and duplicate rows within the residue (documented at judges 19). The Jamieson tree should be re-fetched wholesale.

Scraped page chrome present at exodus 12:51, as predicted. The sweep filed at judges 19 found 1,100 of 1,189 chapters carrying StudyLight.org page furniture inside a Charles Ellicott block, 870 of them on the chapter's last verse. exodus 12 conforms exactly: 983 junk words at v51, the chapter's final verse, inside Ellicott's block. CONSEQUENCE, MEASURED ON THIS CHAPTER: synthesis-loop.py size reported 46,529 usable source words; the real figure is about 45,546. This is the first chapter in the loop where the inflation could have changed a scheduling decision under the owner's 40,000-word rule — it did not here, since both figures are over the line, but a chapter reporting 40,800 would be under it in reality. NOTE ALSO a second, unrelated tail defect visible in this chapter: Gill's block at v51 ends with sacred-texts.com navigation ('Next: Exodus Chapter 13 Sacred Texts | Bible - Previous: John Gill's Exposition of the Entire Bible... Index Next: ...'). That is a different host and a different marker set from the Ellicott/StudyLight problem, and it will NOT be caught by the detector proposed at judges 19. A corpus sweep for 'Sacred Texts | Bible', 'sacred-texts', and the 'Next: ... Index Next:' navigation pattern in Gill blocks should be run alongside the StudyLight sweep before either is used to clean the tree.

SECOND SCRAPED-CHROME DEFECT, MEASURED. Following the exodus 12:51 observation I swept the cow tree for the markers 'Sacred Texts | Bible', 'sacred-texts' and the navigation pattern 'Index Next:'. RESULT: 110 chapters affected, 109,956 junk words, an average of about 1,000 per affected chapter, and every single occurrence falls inside a JOHN GILL block — 110 of 110, no other voice. 105 of the 110 sit on the chapter's last verse. This is a second, independent instance of the same failure mode already documented for Ellicott/StudyLight (1,100 chapters, 1.44M words): the scraper captured the host page's own navigation furniture along with the commentary, and it lands at the end of the last block the voice has in the chapter. The two defects are DISJOINT IN VOICE AND HOST — Ellicott from StudyLight.org, Gill from sacred-texts.com — which means the corpus was assembled from at least two different scrapes with the same bug, and that any cleanup must sweep for both marker sets rather than one. Combined totals across both defects: about 1,210 chapter-verses carrying roughly 1.55 million junk words, inflating every reported usable-source-word figure by 1,000 to 2,300 words per chapter depending on whether one or both voices are hit. Fix for both is identical and needs no re-fetch: truncate the voice block at the first marker, since genuine commentary always precedes it. Worth also sweeping for a third host before concluding the list is complete — two independent instances found in two consecutive batches is not strong evidence that there are only two.

Calvin twice refuses a typological reading available to him in the same chapter, and says so explicitly. At v4-6, on why the flesh was roasted and not boiled: 'I prefer to be ignorant as to why He required the flesh to be roasted and not boiled, rather than to invent such unfounded subtleties, as that Christ was, in a manner, roasted on the Cross.' At v46, on the unbroken bone: 'I am not certain why God desired no bone to be broken... For I fear there is too much subtlety in the explanation which some give, that the virtue of Christ, which is represented by the bones, is not diminished whilst we feed on His flesh' — offering instead the plain suggestion that it was a further sign of haste. This is notable because Calvin is elsewhere in this same chapter the most freely typological voice in the catena (the lamb's perfection showing forth the celestial purity of Christ at v5, the passover answering to the Holy Supper at v24, the paschal lamb instructing the ancients about redemption to come at v46). So the refusals are not a general reticence about typology but a discrimination within it: he accepts the figure where the New Testament itself draws it and refuses it where the correspondence rests only on a physical detail of the rite. That distinction was preserved in both entries rather than flattened, since it is one of the few places in this corpus where a commentator states a criterion for when a type may be pressed. Compare Clarke at judges 19:42, who suppressed part of his own commentary and refused to apologise, and Clarke at exodus 28:42, who allowed only four general senses and warned against being wise above what is written — three separate instances now of commentators drawing an explicit line around allegory.

Four-to-one split on the length of the Egyptian sojourn at v40, with Ellicott alone defending the Hebrew. Clarke calls the statement 'extremely difficult' on all hands, reports Kennicott's rejection of two harmonisations — extending Egypt to include Canaan, and stretching 'the children of Israel' to cover Israel, Isaac and part of Abraham's life, of which Kennicott says 'by this method of reckoning we might arrive at anything but truth, which we may presume was never thus conveyed by an inspired writer' — and adopts the Samaritan Pentateuch's longer reading ('and of their fathers... in the land of Canaan and in the land of Egypt'), supported by the Alexandrian Greek and by Paul, giving 215 years in Canaan plus 215 in Egypt. Gill reports the same expansions from the Greek, the Samaritan, both Talmuds and Aben Ezra and states flatly that Israel was not in Egypt much above 200 years. Calvin independently puts the maximum at 230. Against all three, Ellicott renders the plain Hebrew 'which they sojourned in Egypt' and defends 430 years in Egypt with two supports that do not depend on each other: the prophecy to Abraham that his seed should be a stranger in a land not theirs and serve them 400 years, which he takes of Egypt and not Canaan, and the genealogy of Joshua placing him in the eleventh generation from Jacob, noting that the other genealogies are more or less abbreviated. This is the cleanest textual-versus-internal-evidence disagreement encountered in this corpus so far: three voices resolve it by preferring a variant reading, one by defending the received text from independent data. Carried as an explicit debate.

JFB donor residue at a single position, breaking the stride pattern recorded for the last nineteen chapters. The Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block at verse 1 is an exposition of Shiloh in Genesis 49:10 — the sent, the seed, the peaceable one, the Messiah, and the observation that the Jews have been eighteen centuries without a ruler since Shiloh came. Nothing in it touches Exodus at all, and unlike the residue in genesis 31, genesis 35, genesis 38, exodus 6, exodus 22, leviticus 6, numbers 14 and acts 27, there is no second or third position six verses later: JFB appears nowhere else in this chapter's twenty-nine keys. That makes this the first single-instance case in the run and the first where the donor material comes from a different book rather than a neighbouring chapter. It is worth checking whether the single-instance form and the stride form share a cause, since a stride of six through a chapter with only one JFB key would present exactly this way.

StudyLight chrome tail on the chapter's last verse, now nine for nine across nine books and both testaments (exodus 14:31, genesis 31:54, leviticus 6:30, numbers 14:45, acts 27:44, exodus 22:31, genesis 38:30, genesis 35:29, and here). The Ellicott block at verse 29 gives two usable sentences on the chapter division being unfortunate and the interview running on into the next chapter, then breaks into the site footer, stylesheet and navigation menus. Nine consecutive terminal verses is past the point where per-chapter stripping is the right remedy; the fetcher is not detecting the end of the commentary body on the last key of a chapter, and that is where it should be fixed.

Second instance of the empty Keil block recorded for genesis 35 in note 576, and it confirms the diagnosis. At verse 22 the harvested Keil block is the bare text of verses 22 to 27 followed by a single sentence of comment that belongs to verse 28; at verse 28 the block is nothing but the text of verses 28 and 29, with no comment whatever. The result is that Keil could be given a place in the 21-23 entry only by using the one displaced sentence about Pharaoh's wrath, and that the 24-29 entry had to exclude him outright — the only exclusion in this chapter besides the JFB residue. Clarke's block at verse 1 has the mirror-image fault, opening with the whole chapter argument as a table of contents before any comment begins. Both are paragraph-boundary faults in the harvest rather than defects in the sources themselves, and both are now attested in two books.

The discipline proposed at the end of note 577 was tried on this chapter and it works, though it does not solve the problem. For every one of the seven entries the items were listed from the dump and struck to about twelve before a sentence was written. First drafts came in at 918, 927, 935, 938, 953, 954 and 979 QA words against a 650 ceiling — an average overshoot of 45 per cent, which is no better than genesis 35, but the shape of the trimming changed. Where the earlier chapters needed eight to eleven passes each and lost five to nine words a pass, these needed four to seven, and the first pass in each case removed 90 to 180 words by dropping whole items that had already been identified as the weakest. The residual overshoot is not a selection failure but a length-estimation failure: twelve items of grounded prose from five or six voices simply runs to about 900 words, so the real target is nine items, not twelve. That is the number to try next.

JFB donor residue at stride 6, five positions, the cleanest instance of the pattern recorded so far. The Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks fall at verses 4, 10, 16, 22 and 28 — every sixth verse from 4 to the end of a twenty-nine-verse chapter, with no other JFB key anywhere in it. None of the five touches Deuteronomy. Verses 4 and 10 carry one and the same block on Israel presuming to go up the hill after the report of the spies (Numbers 14); verse 16 carries a note on the omer as the tenth part of an ephah; verse 22 a note on the proportions of the meat offering; verse 28 a note on the proselyte's share in Israel's privileges. This is the twentieth consecutive chapter with the fault, and the first where the stride is visible across five positions with nothing else present to obscure it. Taken with the single-instance case at exodus 10:1, where the chapter had only one JFB key, the natural reading is that the JFB harvest is offset by a fixed step against the verse index and simply lands wherever that step falls.

StudyLight chrome tail on the chapter's last verse, ten for ten across ten books and both testaments. The Ellicott block at verse 29 gives three usable sentences on Beth-peor as Moses' burial-place and on this verse concluding the recapitulation from Horeb, then runs into the site footer, stylesheet and navigation menus; Gill's block at the same verse ends with the chapter index links. Ten consecutive terminal verses, in books as far apart as Genesis and Acts, settles the diagnosis: the fetcher is not detecting the end of the commentary body on a chapter's final key. Every one of these chapters has had to be worked around by hand at the last span.

The nine-item target proposed at the end of note 581 was tried here and is close to right. Four entries were drafted from item lists cut to roughly ten before writing, and the first drafts came in at 923, 940, 966 and 1036 QA words — still 45 to 60 per cent over the 650 ceiling, so ten grounded items from five or six voices continues to run near 950 words. The useful finding is the arithmetic behind it: a grounded item, written as a full sentence with its attribution, costs about ninety words. Nine items is therefore about 810, and seven is about 630. Seven is the number that actually fits, and the entries that trimmed fastest here were the ones where three items were struck outright in the first pass rather than shaved. The counting rule to carry forward is that an entry holds seven items, not nine and not twelve, and that anything past the seventh should be selected only if it is short enough to run as a clause rather than a sentence.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, TWELFTH consecutive chapter and ninth book: keys 5, 11, 17, 23, 29 — offset 5, five members, no gaps. Content is unrelated to Galatians (the v23 block argues Jacob and Esau from Romans 9; the v29 block is on Philippians 2:12-13). Running table: joshua 10 (1,7,13,19,25,37,43), 1corinthians 7 (5,11,17,23,29,35), hebrews 11 (3,9,15,27,33), romans 8 (2,8,14,20,26,32,38), romans 9 (4,22,28), 1corinthians 15 (12,18,24,36,42,48,54), leviticus 27 (4,10,16,22,28,34), judges 16 (9,15,21,27), exodus 28 (1,7,13,37), judges 19 (3,9,15,21,27), exodus 12 (8,14,20,32,38), galatians 4 (5,11,17,23,29). Consistent with a single row pointer walking a canonical index at fixed stride and lagging its target. The Jamieson tree wants a re-fetch.

Patristic verse-misalignment, a defect class not previously recorded. Both patristic blocks filed at galatians 4:1 are commentary on something else: the John Chrysostom block opens 'Ver. 4, 5' and is his note on vv4-5, and the Tertullian block is his anti-Marcion argument on Romans 1:16-18 from Against Marcion — wrong book entirely. Both excluded via EXCL_BY_ENTRY. Consequence: genuine Chrysostom commentary on Gal 4:4-5 is present in the tree but unusable, because the entry that covers vv4-5 has no Chrysostom head of its own. Unlike the Jamieson stride this is not a fixed-offset pattern (one block is off by three verses within the book, the other is from another epistle), so it needs its own sweep.

Third instance of scraped page chrome, and it confirms the attachment model. 926 junk words (StudyLight nav/copyright boilerplate) begin at word 182 of the Charles Ellicott block at galatians 4:30. It sits on v30, NOT on the chapter's last verse v31 — because Ellicott has no block on v31 at all. So the chrome attaches to the VOICE'S last block, not the chapter's last verse, which is why 870 of the 1,100 known StudyLight cases land on the final verse: that is simply where Ellicott usually stops. Corpus totals unchanged: StudyLight/Ellicott 1,100 chapters and ~1.44M junk words; sacred-texts/Gill 110 chapters and ~110k. 'synthesis-loop.py size' does not strip either, so reported usable-source-word figures run 1,000-2,300 high. A third host should still be checked before any cleanup is called complete.

Tooling defect hit while landing this chapter: synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS carries SHORT forms for the fathers and for Robertson ('Chrysostom', 'Robertson', 'Cyril', 'Augustine'), and undeclarable_voices() matches the tags' excluded_voices strings against those short labels. So an exclusion written with the catena's own head — 'John Chrysostom', which is literally what the <strong> head says — fails validate-synthesis.py with 'excluded_voices names a block absent from this entry's source'. Worked around here by emitting the short label. This is the standing VOICE_LABELS item and it now has a concrete failure mode, not just a prose-spelling nuisance: the label list and the catena heads disagree, and the validator sides with the label list.

Three positions worth flagging. (a) Virgin birth at v4: Clarke and Wesley read the miraculous conception out of 'made of a woman', while Ellicott and Robertson both explicitly deny any allusion to it there, Robertson adding that the doctrine is nonetheless compatible with the phrase. (b) Clarke at v6 numbers the Trinity as Father, Spirit, Son, making the Holy Ghost the second person and Christ the third. (c) Barnes stands alone twice: at v6 in denying the Spirit named there is the Holy Spirit, and at v10 in denying the Sabbath is among the days observed.

First use of the 'lutheran' school slug in this loop, and first appearance of Martin Luther and Albert Barnes as voices. Galatians 4 is the densest chapter attempted: 13 distinct voices, ~73,700 real usable source words after subtracting 926 words of chrome, 31 verses, tiled in 13 entries. Luther's Galatians commentary is by a wide margin the largest single block in the chapter (3,188 words at v27 alone) and is polemical throughout, so the lutheran school summaries run long; the tag-side school text is where his argument is carried, with the prose taking only the load-bearing claims.

Four disputes recorded in the tags for this chapter. (1) Whether the allegory is in Moses' text or only in Paul's use of it — Henry allows a further design by the Spirit, Barnes denies any design and treats it as illustration, Calvin threads between. (2) Whether 'Hagar' is genuinely an Arabic name for Sinai — Luther and Gill report the philology as fact and Ellicott concludes for it after an excursus, while Barnes cannot find the word in Castell or Gesenius and denies Paul knew such a sense; Clarke and Barnes both report a manuscript tradition dropping the name from the verse. (3) Where the Jerusalem above is — Barnes and Ellicott celestially, Calvin denying it is contained in heaven at all, Gill making it the gospel church state of the apostle's own day. (4) Whether Ishmael's act amounts to persecution — Calvin insists only ridicule is recorded and asks how far that stands from persecution, while rejecting the reading that makes it a harmless smile; Ellicott doubts the Hebrew means more than playing.

galatians 4: all 13 entries self-graded A, 0 UNSOURCED, 0 fidelity failures. Every first draft again came in over the 650-word ceiling — drafts ran 564 to 1,000 words against the cap and needed one to five trim passes each; entry 24-25 drafted at 905 and 28-31 at 867. The two entries written deliberately spare (6 at 622w, 7 at 564w) landed in a single pass, which is the only reliable countermeasure found so far. Two structural notes on the cross-school citation in this chapter: Ellicott quotes Calvin by name and in full as his warrant for allegorical treatment, and Cyril of Jerusalem and Calvin deploy the identical phrase 'the mother of us all' on opposite sides of the visible-church question.

JFB stride-6 donor residue, twenty-first consecutive chapter. Seven JFB keys at vv.5/17/23/29/41/47/53 — every sixth verse — and every one of them carries matter belonging to Leviticus 7, 8, 15 and 16, none of it to chapter 25. Read with exodus 10 (a SINGLE JFB key at v1 carrying Genesis 49:10 matter) and deuteronomy 3 (five keys at vv.4/10/16/22/28, all Numbers 14 matter), the diagnosis is settled: the JFB harvest is offset by a fixed step against the verse index and lands wherever that step falls, which accounts for both the stride form and the single-instance form. JFB is therefore excluded from nine of this chapter's ten entries as undeclarable, and that exclusion is correct, not a drafting gap.

StudyLight chrome tail on the chapter's LAST verse — eleven for eleven now (exodus 14:31, genesis 31:54, leviticus 6:30, numbers 14:45, acts 27:44, exodus 22:31, genesis 38:30, genesis 35:29, exodus 10:29, deuteronomy 3:29, leviticus 25:55). The fetcher is not detecting the end of the commentary body on a chapter's final key. This is a harvest-side fix and has now been recommended eleven times; it is cheap to make and would clean every chapter at once.

Displaced Keil blocks, now attested in a fourth book. Keil's v21 block opens with the raw verse text of vv.21-23 before any comment, and the comment when it comes is on v23; his v45 block runs the verse text of vv.45-47 before commenting on v47; his v48 block runs the text of vv.48-52 and then comments on v51. In each case the exposition is real and usable but is filed one to four verses ahead of the material it treats. This is the same paragraph-boundary fault recorded for genesis 35 and exodus 10 (notes 576, 580) — the harvest breaks the block at the wrong place, not the source. Consequence for drafting: Keil looked absent from the vv.20-23 and vv.44-50 entries on a first read and was only recovered by opening the raw blocks after the ghost script flagged him.

Three voice omissions in one chapter, all caught by the ghost script rather than by the pre-draft voice profile: Ellicott from the vv.8-10 entry (he has substantial material at all three verses — the count-seven-weeks-of-years gloss, the rams'-horn cornets, and the forgiven-debts moral of the atonement day), and Keil from the vv.20-23 and vv.44-50 entries (both displaced blocks, see the companion note). Note 569 set the rule that the voice profile should be run BEFORE drafting and the list of present voices kept beside the draft; on a ten-entry chapter that rule was followed for the chapter but not re-checked per entry, which is where all three slipped. The refinement: on chapters of eight or more entries the present-voice list must be checked per ENTRY at the end of each draft, not once for the chapter. All three were restored and paid for by dropping whole items elsewhere; the chapter landed at 634-650 QA words with no ghosts.

The batch rule budgets by SOURCE WORDS, but entry count is what actually drives the work. Leviticus 25 passed the word budget comfortably (33,347 usable source words, well under the ~40,000 whole-batch threshold) and yet took ten entries, because it has 55 source keys with a median of 457 words each. Compare exodus 10: 24,384 words but only 29 keys and seven entries. At a similar word budget leviticus 25 was roughly 1.4x the drafting work and, because every entry needs its own trim-to-650 loop and its own voice check, closer to 2x the elapsed effort. Recommendation: 'synthesis-loop.py size' should also report a projected entry count (source words / ~3,300, or keys / ~5) alongside the word total, since entry count is the better predictor of whether a chapter can be finished in one sitting — and an abandoned pick costs the run everything.

Drafting arithmetic, confirmed again over ten entries. A grounded item written as a full attributed sentence costs ~90-110 words, so seven items is the number that fits under the 650-word QA ceiling; five items lands near 670 and six near 740, both of which still need trimming. Measured trim passes on this chapter: the eight-item entry took 14 passes, the six-item entries took 4, the five-item entries took 2. The cheapest correction remains dropping a whole item rather than shaving clauses — clause-shaving costs three or four passes to recover the same words and flattens the prose while doing it.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTEENTH consecutive chapter and tenth book: keys 3, 9, 15, 21, 27 — offset 3, five members, no gaps. This instance is the strongest evidence yet for the row-pointer theory, because all five blocks are ONE CONTIGUOUS PASSAGE walked in narrative order: they are Jamieson on Acts 16, the Philippi jail episode — v3 the charge before the magistrates, v9 the midnight singing of praises, v15 the graphic detail about the jailer, v21 the magistrates relenting, v27 their coming in person to bring the prisoners out. Not random misfiling: a single pointer sampling one source region at fixed stride. Running table now: joshua 10, 1corinthians 7, hebrews 11, romans 8, romans 9, 1corinthians 15, leviticus 27, judges 16, exodus 28, judges 19, exodus 12, galatians 4, 1corinthians 1. The Jamieson tree needs a re-fetch.

John Lightfoot (new voice this batch, assigned school 'puritan-evangelical' as a Westminster Assembly divine) has three blocks in this chapter that belong to OTHER CHAPTERS of the same epistle, filed by verse number with the chapter component lost: 1:6 holds his note on 2:6 ('Yet the wisdom not of this world'), 1:8 holds his note on 4:8 ('Now ye are full'), 1:13 holds his note on 3:13 ('For the day shall declare it'). The eight other Lightfoot blocks here (1, 2, 5, 12, 14, 17, 20, 21) are correctly filed. Chapters 2 and 4 of 1corinthians carry NO Lightfoot blocks at all, and chapter 3 has only verses 1 and 5 — consistent with displacement into chapter 1 rather than duplication. A related out-of-range symptom: 1corinthians 16.json has a Lightfoot key '55', but that chapter has only 24 verses, so it is 15:55 material. Worth a corpus-wide sweep for Lightfoot keys exceeding a chapter's verse count.

Cyril of Jerusalem's blocks in this chapter are FOUR distinct texts spread over EIGHT verse keys — the repeated-block defect previously seen at 1corinthians 15. Block A (twofold purification, water and Spirit) sits at v2 and v13; block B (on 'he blinded the thoughts of them that believe not', which is 2 Cor 4:4, not this chapter) sits at v7, v8 and v10; block C (glory in the Cross) at v18 and v23; block D (transfer from Catechumens to the Faithful, quoting 1:9 exactly) at v9 alone. Blocks A, C and D land on apt verses; block B is misfiled from another epistle and triplicated. Used A at 13-16, C at 18-19, D at 7-9; dropped B at 10-12 and the duplicate of C at 22-25.

The VOICE_LABELS defect is worse than last batch's instance and now has TWO failure modes, both hit here. (1) The list carries short forms, so an exclusion written with the catena's own head fails: 'John Lightfoot' must be declared as 'Lightfoot', 'John Chrysostom' as 'Chrysostom'. (2) Far worse — 'Cyril of Jerusalem' can NEVER be declared at all. _LABEL_RE is built as '(label)\s*:' and the list holds only the bare 'Cyril', so the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' matches nothing; split_voices() does not report Cyril as present in any blob, and undeclarable_voices() therefore rejects EVERY spelling of the exclusion. The only way to drop a Cyril block is to omit it silently, which loses the audit trail the excluded_voices field exists to provide. Two Cyril blocks in this chapter had to be dropped that way. Fix: spell the fathers in full in VOICE_LABELS (or match the longest label first), which would also fix the prose-spelling nuisance in one go.

Two further filing observations. (a) Albert Barnes' block at 1:1 is the epistle's whole front matter (situation of Corinth, establishment of the church, time and place of writing, occasion) and ends with a printed pointer, 'Remainder of Introductory Notes and Information on Verse 1 located in 1 Corinthians 1:2'; his v2 block continues that introduction and only then carries his actual verse notes for BOTH v1 and v2. So a per-verse entry at 1:1 would find no Barnes comment on the verse at all. The pericope tiling absorbed it, since the entry's source is the union of vv1-3, but a one-verse tiling here would have silently lost him. (b) Page chrome: 926 junk words (StudyLight boilerplate) begin at word 182 of the Charles Ellicott block at 1:31, which is both the chapter's last verse and Ellicott's last block — consistent with the attachment model recorded at galatians 4:30.

Adam Clarke reproduces John Lightfoot's notes verbatim and under his name THREE times in this chapter — on Gaius and the Johannine epistles at v14, on the four titles at v20, and on 'the wisdom of God' meaning wisdom ABOUT God rather than wisdom FROM God at v21. Where both voices are in the same entry this makes them a single witness rather than two, and the prose says so rather than counting the agreement twice. Lightfoot's own chain at v14 is the boldest reasoning in the chapter: if the Gaius of 3 John is the Corinthian Gaius, then 1 John was written to the Corinthians.

Four disputes worth flagging from this chapter. (1) At v13, whether 'Is Christ divided?' is a question at all: Ellicott reads it as a statement, Gill reports both punctuations and answers no, Robertson thinks it probably interrogative and records that Hofmann called the assertory form a rhetorical impossibility. (2) At v20, whether the triple question quotes Isaiah: Calvin denies it outright and says Paul speaks in his own person, since the passage usually cited has nothing to do with the subject, while Gill and Barnes allow familiar prophetic language used without intent to quote. (3) At v25, a precise clash: Ellicott insists the sense is 'wiser than men themselves' and NOT 'wiser than the wisdom of men', naming the latter as the view of some — and Robertson supplies exactly that rejected reading, calling it a condensed comparison and a common Greek idiom. (4) At v26, the mood of the opening verb: Ellicott and Clarke read an imperative, Robertson notes the form is identical for both, and Calvin expressly leaves the choice to the reader because nothing in the sense turns on it.

1corinthians 1: all 11 entries self-graded A, 0 UNSOURCED, 0 fidelity failures. 31 verses, ~77,650 real usable source words after subtracting 926 words of chrome, tiled in 11 entries — exactly the count the density guide predicts. 13 distinct voices, including John Lightfoot for the first time in this loop; entry 1-3 carries 12 of them in 646 words, the densest single entry written so far. The overshoot pattern held again and was worst where the voice count was highest: entry 1-3 drafted at 1,051 words against the 650 ceiling and needed three passes; 26-29 drafted at 810, 13-16 at 880, 30-31 at 802. Every one of the eleven first drafts was over. The only reliable countermeasure remains drafting deliberately spare, and at twelve voices in one entry even that fails.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, FOURTEENTH consecutive chapter and eleventh book: keys 12, 18, 24 — offset 0, three members, no gaps. Same signature as 1corinthians 1: all three blocks come from ONE contiguous source region rather than being scattered. Here it is Numbers 27-28 — v12 is on Moses asking God for a successor ('the Author of all the intellectual gifts... who can raise up qualified persons for the most arduous duties'), v18 on Joshua honoured and qualified through the high priest asking counsel by Urim (Num 27:15-21), v24 on the repetition of formerly enacted laws and the appointed offerings (Num 28). Running table: joshua 10, 1corinthians 7, hebrews 11, romans 8, romans 9, 1corinthians 15, leviticus 27, judges 16, exodus 28, judges 19, exodus 12, galatians 4, 1corinthians 1, deuteronomy 22. Two independent chapters now show the contiguous-region signature; the row-pointer diagnosis is as well evidenced as it can get without a re-fetch.

Third host confirmed for the scraped page-chrome defect, and it is the sacred-texts one rather than a new one: 27 junk words ('Sacred Texts | Bible' nav) at the tail of the John Gill block on deuteronomy 22:30 — the chapter's last verse and Gill's last block, matching the attachment model recorded at galatians 4:30 and 1corinthians 1:31. Only 27 words here, so this chapter's size figure is barely inflated, but it confirms the sacred-texts/Gill defect reaches the Pentateuch and is not confined to the 110 chapters previously counted. The corpus scan for that marker should be re-run: the earlier count may have used a stricter marker set.

Four disputes worth flagging. (1) At v5, what the forbidden thing is: Clarke narrows it to armour, arguing that a mere change of dress could not have disguised anyone where both sexes wore long garments; Keil widens it to every kind of domestic utensil, neither clothing merely nor arms only; Gill takes it of a man's working instruments and reads the law as a rebuke of Egyptian practice reported by Herodotus. (2) At v12, what the fringes were for: Ellicott makes them a memorial of the man executed for sabbath-breaking and Wesley adds a national profession, while CALVIN REFUSES the memorial entirely and makes the fringe a device of decency, holding the open gown closed — a reading none of the others entertains. (3) At v17, whether the evidence in the slander case is intelligible: Henry and Wesley agree almost verbatim that the learned are not agreed and it is unnecessary to enquire, while Clarke refuses to leave it there and dismisses the metaphorical readings as failing so completely that setting them out would waste the reader's time. (4) At v30, how far the single incest prohibition reaches: Clarke restricts it to a stepmother, Gill treats it as a 'short memorandum' standing for the whole Levitical law, and Calvin reasons from the same silence that the fuller law is being recalled under one head.

deuteronomy 22: all 7 entries self-graded A, 0 UNSOURCED, 0 fidelity failures. 30 verses, ~14,700 usable source words, tiled in 7 entries — matching the density guide. 8 voices, the largest single blocks being Henry at v5 (1,423w) and v13 (1,486w). NOTABLE CONTRAST with the last four batches: on a thin-source chapter the overshoot problem largely disappears. Three of the seven entries (1-4 at 487w, 22-27 at 583w, 28-30 at 516w) landed in window on the FIRST draft with no trim pass at all — the first time that has happened in this loop. The other four needed one to three passes. The pattern across recent chapters is now clear: overshoot scales with source density and voice count, not with chapter length. Where the source gives 1,500-1,800 words per entry the draft lands naturally; where it gives 7,000+ and ten or more voices, every draft runs 20-60 percent over.

JFB stride-6 donor residue, twenty-second consecutive chapter. Four JFB keys at vv.11/17/23/29 — every sixth verse — and every one carries matter from Genesis 41 (Joseph's investiture with the signet-ring, khelaat and gold necklace; the naming of his children; the seventeen years and the storehouses), none of it touching chapter 49 at any point. JFB is therefore excluded as undeclarable from the four entries whose spans contain those keys, and that exclusion is correct rather than a drafting gap. The fixed-step diagnosis recorded at leviticus 25 holds exactly here.

StudyLight chrome tail on the chapter's LAST verse — twelve for twelve now (exodus 14:31, genesis 31:54, leviticus 6:30, numbers 14:45, acts 27:44, exodus 22:31, genesis 38:30, genesis 35:29, exodus 10:29, deuteronomy 3:29, leviticus 25:55, genesis 49:33). Here it is Ellicott's v33 block, which runs several kilobytes of site navigation, CSS and a commentary index after two sentences of exposition. Twelve recommendations for the same harvest-side fix; it is cheap to make and would clean every chapter at once.

Keil's blocks are displaced through the WHOLE of this chapter, not at isolated points. Every one opens with the raw verse text of two or three verses and then comments on the LAST of them, so his exposition sits one to two verses before the material it treats: the v2 block comments on the last days (v1); the v4 block on Simeon and Levi (vv.5-6); the v6 block on Judah (v8); the v10 block on the vine (vv.11-12); the v12 block on Zebulun (v13); the v26 block on Benjamin (v27). This is the paragraph-boundary fault recorded for genesis 35, exodus 10 and leviticus 25 (notes 576, 580, 592), but sustained across an entire chapter for the first time. Practical cost here: Keil's geographical note on Zebulun — that the tribe's territory neither reached the Mediterranean nor touched Zidon, which bears directly on Ellicott's argument in the vv.1-2 entry — is filed at v12 while Keil has no key at v13, so it could not be used in any entry without crediting him in a span where he has no key. That material is simply lost to the harvest defect.

Working rule adopted for systematically displaced blocks, and worth ratifying or overruling. Where a source's block is shifted by the harvest, the material is used in the entry whose verses it actually TREATS, provided that source has a key inside that span; where it has no key there, the voice is excluded and the material dropped. Applied here: Keil's Simeon-and-Levi exposition (filed v4) went into the vv.5-6 entry, where he has a key at v6; his vine exposition (filed v10) into the vv.11-12 entry, where he has a key at v12. Keil is therefore legitimately excluded from the vv.3-4 and v10 entries, whose keys hold only verse text. This keeps every attribution grounded in a key inside its own span while keeping the prose topically honest — the plain filing rule of note 449 would have put Simeon and Levi inside the Reuben entry. Henry and Clarke were handled by the plain rule instead, because their whole-pericope overviews at a span's first verse are the case that rule was written for and they have no keys further on.

The entry-count problem, stated with the worst case yet. Genesis 49 is 47,985 usable source words across 33 keys — over the 40,000-word whole-batch threshold, so it was correctly taken as the entire batch — but the number that governed the work was FIFTEEN entries, not the word count. Verse 10 alone runs 5,638 source words, v1 4,139 and v8 4,063, so three keys had to stand almost alone under the 4,500-word span rule; the median key is 963 words, five times the median of an ordinary chapter. Compare exodus 10 at 24,384 words in seven entries, or leviticus 25 at 33,347 in ten. Recommendation, now made twice: 'synthesis-loop.py size' should report a projected entry count alongside the word total — keys divided by about two for a chapter with this median, or source words divided by about 3,200 — because entry count, not word count, is what determines whether a chapter can be carried to landing in one sitting, and an abandoned pick costs the run everything.

Trim-pass measurement over fifteen entries, the largest sample yet in one chapter. First drafts came in at 780-990 QA words against a 650 ceiling, needing 4 to 19 trim passes each; the two heaviest (the vv.24-26 and vv.29-33 entries, 17 and 19 passes) were both cases where five source voices each had two substantial items. The arithmetic of note 589 held again — roughly 90-100 words per grounded attributed item, so seven items is the ceiling — but the finding this chapter adds is that with SIX voices present the seven-item budget forces one voice to a single clause, and that voice is then the one the ghost script flags. Three exclusions had to be repaired after assembly for exactly that reason (Ellicott, Keil, Wesley in earlier chapters; Wesley and Keil here). The cheaper order is: fix the item budget per VOICE before drafting — one substantial item each for six voices, one extra for the two carrying the chapter's dispute — rather than drafting to the word count and rescuing voices afterwards.

Clarke's v33 block carries a displaced excursus of the kind recorded at genesis 38:30 (note 568): some nine hundred words mapping the twelve sons onto the signs of the Zodiac, after Vallancy and Hales — Reuben to Aquarius, Simeon and Levi to Gemini, Judah to Leo, Asher to Virgo, Issachar to Taurus, Dan to Scorpio, Joseph to Sagittarius, Naphtali to Aries, Zebulun to Cancer, Gad to Pisces, Benjamin to Capricorn — followed by Clarke's own disclaimer, 'What likelihood the reader may see in all this, I cannot pretend to say.' It is filed at the death of Jacob, has nothing to do with vv.29-33, and the author disowns it in the same breath; left unused, and recorded here so the next worker on this chapter does not spend time deciding about it twice.

Pick declined before drafting, and no chapter taken this batch. philippians 2 sizes at 62,574 usable source words across 30 keys, median 1,981 — the heaviest chapter measured to date. Three keys individually exceed the ~4,500-word span limit of note 449 (v1 5,439; v6 5,074; v30 4,527), so each must stand alone, and a legal tiling needs roughly fifteen to seventeen entries — more drafting than genesis 49 (47,985 words, 15 entries) which had just consumed a full working window. Eight further picks were sampled to see whether the queue offered anything smaller: acts 17 (84,788), acts 7 (97,718), ephesians 4 (73,597), galatians 3 (108,108), 1corinthians 11 (70,342, twice), deuteronomy 33 (41,858), and numbers 31 (19,991, blocked pending the owner's decision on its source file). Every unblocked option is over the 40,000-word whole-batch threshold and none is under fifteen entries. Declined under the standing rule that an abandoned pick costs the run everything and the queue nothing. Recorded so the next worker knows the repair queue head is now uniformly 60k-110k words and that --worst-first has drained everything smaller: the queue needs either a fresh worker per chapter or a way to split a chapter across sessions.

Offered again by the picker this batch (19,991 source words across 42 keys — by far the smallest unfinished repair left in the queue) and passed over per the standing instruction that it is blocked pending an owner decision on its source file. Noting the recurrence because it is now the only pick under the 40,000-word threshold that the picker produces: while it stays blocked, every batch is forced onto a 60,000-word-plus chapter.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, FIFTEENTH consecutive chapter and twelfth book: keys 4, 10, 16, 22, 28 — offset 4, five members, no gaps. THIRD chapter to show the contiguous-region signature, after 1corinthians 1 (Acts 16) and deuteronomy 22 (Numbers 27-28). Here the source region is GALATIANS 1-2, walked in order: v4 is on Gal 2:20 ('gave himself for me'), v10 on Gal 1:9 ('if any man preach any other gospel'), v16 on Gal 1:14 ('I profited beyond those of mine own age among my countrymen'), v22 on Gal 1:19 and Acts 9:27-28, v28 on Gal 1:23-24 ('the former wolf is now acting the shepherd's part'). Three independent chapters now show one pointer sampling a single contiguous region at fixed stride; the diagnosis is settled as far as it can be without a re-fetch. Running table: joshua 10, 1corinthians 7, hebrews 11, romans 8, romans 9, 1corinthians 15, leviticus 27, judges 16, exodus 28, judges 19, exodus 12, galatians 4, 1corinthians 1, deuteronomy 22, hebrews 12.

Cyril of Jerusalem appears at four keys in this chapter (2, 16, 21, 22) with FOUR DISTINCT blocks and no duplicates — the first chapter in this loop where his blocks are all unique and all apt to their verses: the Son's session at the right hand for 12:2, the doctrine of chastity for the Esau warning at 12:16, the Jews who read but do not hear for the Sinai passage at 12:21, and the congregations of Israel giving way to a Church built from the Gentiles for 12:22. John Chrysostom likewise has five distinct and on-topic blocks (4, 11, 14, 18, 28). This is worth recording because it shows the patristic duplication defect seen at 1corinthians 1 and 1corinthians 15 is not universal, so a corpus sweep for it should be by-chapter rather than assumed global.

Four disputes worth flagging. (1) At v6, whether 'whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth' states a universal rule: Barnes takes it as one and guards it twice, while CALVIN RAISES THE OBJECTION AGAINST HIS OWN TEXT — 'this seems not to be a well-founded reason', since God visits elect and reprobate indiscriminately and his scourges manifest wrath oftener than love, as Scripture speaks and experience confirms — answering only that when the godly are addressed the effect they feel is alone in view. (2) At v18, what they could not endure: Barnes says the commands were not intolerable and locates the terror in the manner of communication, while Gill locates it in the law itself, as a yoke of bondage and a covenant of works giving no strength to perform. (3) At v25-26, whose voice shook the earth at Sinai: Gill and Clarke both say Christ's, Clarke recording that others refer it simply to the Father. (4) At v27, what the removal means: Clarke reads it historically of the Jewish polity, already shaking under Roman power, and denies God ever designed that religion to become general; Ellicott insists the words 'must of necessity' point to the final change; Wesley makes it heaven and earth replaced by the new. Also at v21 a source problem: Barnes states plainly that the words attributed to Moses are not in the Exodus narrative and that the apostle's authority for them has been questioned, while Ellicott finds part of them in the Greek of Deuteronomy but on a later occasion.

hebrews 12: all 9 entries self-graded A, 0 UNSOURCED, 0 fidelity failures. 29 verses, ~62,765 real usable source words after subtracting 926 words of StudyLight chrome in the Ellicott block at v29, tiled in 9 entries — matching the density guide exactly. 11 voices; the largest blocks are Henry at v4 (3,148w) and v18 (2,746w) and Barnes at v1 (2,121w). Overshoot confirmed the rule recorded at deuteronomy 22: it scales with voice count, not chapter length. The two 8-voice-or-fewer entries drafted closest to window (12-13 at 675 first-draft, and it alone needed just one pass to reach 578), while the 9- and 10-voice entries drafted at 842, 850, 876, 919 and 925 words against the 650 ceiling and needed two to four passes each. Entry 25-29 drafted at 925, the worst first draft of the batch.

JFB stride donor residue, twenty-third consecutive chapter, and the first NT instance measured in this run. Four JFB keys at vv.3/9/15/27 — a stride of six from 3 to 9 to 15, then a gap at 21 and a resumption at 27 — and every one carries matter from a different chapter of Acts: v3 the upper room and the five hundred brethren of Acts 1, vv.9 and 15 the Pentecost reckoning of Acts 2, v27 a bare fragment of the same. None of it touches chapter 22 at any point. The gap at v21 is new: the stride skips one position rather than running unbroken, which fits the fixed-step diagnosis if the donor chapter simply has no key at the corresponding offset. JFB is excluded as undeclarable from the four entries whose spans hold those keys.

StudyLight chrome tail on the chapter's LAST verse — thirteen for thirteen (exodus 14:31, genesis 31:54, leviticus 6:30, numbers 14:45, acts 27:44, exodus 22:31, genesis 38:30, genesis 35:29, exodus 10:29, deuteronomy 3:29, leviticus 25:55, genesis 49:33, acts 22:30). Here it is Ellicott's v30 block, which breaks off after two sentences of exposition into several kilobytes of site navigation, CSS and a commentary index. Thirteen recommendations now for the same harvest-side fix.

Cyril of Jerusalem is donor residue throughout this chapter, and the ghost script does NOT catch it. Four Cyril keys, none touching Acts 22: v6 and v17 both carry the same Antioch passage from the Catechetical Lectures (Barnabas sent to Antioch, Paul brought from Tarsus, the disciples first called Christians there — Acts 11 and 13 matter); v10 carries a lecture against the Jews on the Father and the Son; v16 carries the proclamation of the divine name to Moses in Exodus 34. All four are excluded, but because synthesis_qa.undeclarable_voices() does not recognise them as undeclarable, the ghost report lists Cyril under missing with an empty excl list, so the exclusion is never recorded in the tags. Two consequences worth acting on: the drafter must open every Cyril block by hand rather than trusting the excl column, and undeclarable_voices() would be worth extending to catch a block whose scripture references all fall outside the chapter being worked.

Barnes and Gill both degrade to bare cross-references across the vision dialogue. Barnes at vv.7, 8, 9, 10, 13 carries nothing but a pointer — 'Acts 9:3 and Acts 9:4-7' — with no comment at all, and Gill at vv.7, 8, 10 gives only a truncated 'See Gill on' whose target is missing from the harvest. The effect is that in the vv.7-11 entry Barnes has five consecutive keys and no usable prose, so he is correctly excluded, and Gill survives only on the strength of two short remarks at vv.9 and 11. This is the same empty-block class recorded for Keil in the Pentateuch (notes 576, 580, 592, 606), but with a different cause: here the commentator genuinely wrote a cross-reference rather than the harvest breaking a paragraph. It still costs the entry a voice, and it is worth distinguishing the two cases when the harvest is next revised — a real cross-reference cannot be recovered by refetching, whereas a broken paragraph can.

Chrysostom's only key in the chapter is at v17, and his comment runs from v17 through v25 — eight verses ahead of where it is filed. Under the working rule proposed at genesis 49 (note 607), his vv.17-21 matter was used in the vv.16-17 entry, where he has a key and where the content belongs; his vv.22-25 matter could not be used at all, since he has no key in either the v22 or the vv.23-25 span. That is a real loss: his reading of the tribune's conduct — that he ought to have learnt from the clamourers and asked whether they laid hold on anything spoken, but instead indulged his arbitrary pleasure, looking not to what was righteous but to how he might stop their unrighteous rage — is the sharpest comment any voice makes on that scene, and no other source says it. Recording it as the first measured cost of the rule in the NT corpus, and as a second argument for repairing the harvest's paragraph boundaries rather than working around them.

Entry-count sizing, third measurement and the first that came out right. acts 22 is 36,246 usable source words across 30 keys, median 696 — under the 40,000 whole-batch threshold — and only one key (v3, 8,091 words) exceeds the 4,500-word span limit, so it tiled to ELEVEN entries. Compare genesis 49 at 47,985 words in fifteen entries and philippians 2, declined last batch at 62,574 words in a projected fifteen to seventeen. The predictor that would have worked here is keys divided by median band: a chapter whose median key is under about 800 words tiles at roughly keys/3, while one with a median near 1,000 tiles at roughly keys/2, and one with a median near 2,000 tiles at nearly one entry per key. Recommendation, now made three times: have 'synthesis-loop.py size' print the median key length and a projected entry count beside the word total. Word count alone has now mis-signalled the workload in both directions.

Jamieson stride-6 defect, SIXTEENTH consecutive chapter. Keys 3, 9, 15, 27 - stride 6 from offset 3, four members, ONE GAP at 21. All four blocks are headless mid-sentence fragments (79, 26, 27 and 6 words) and all four are on Acts 2 (Pentecost): v3 on the disciples' expectant prayer and the five hundred brethren; v9 on the fiftieth day from the morrow after the Passover sabbath; v15 on the Parthians and Medes not permanently settled there; v27 the six-word fragment 'in advance, perhaps, of the rest'. This is the FOURTH chapter showing the contiguous-region signature - one pointer sampling a single contiguous source region at fixed stride (cf. 1corinthians 1 on Acts 16, deuteronomy 22 on Numbers 27-28, hebrews 12 on Galatians 1-2). Diagnosis is settled as far as it can be without a re-fetch of the Jamieson tree.

John Lightfoot chapter-component loss: his only block in this chapter, filed at 22:1, is on the Sadducees and their canon, which belongs to Acts 23:6-8. Acts 22 never mentions the Sadducees. Same defect class as 1corinthians 1 (1:6=2:6, 1:8=4:8, 1:13=3:13) and 1corinthians 16 (key 55 in a 24-verse chapter). Excluded by entry.

Cyril of Jerusalem: four blocks in this chapter, ALL off-topic, and v17 duplicates v6 verbatim. v6/v17 are on Barnabas sent to Antioch and the disciples first called Christians there (Acts 11); v10 is catechesis on God the Father; v16 is on Moses and the divine name. All dropped silently rather than declared, because Cyril is UNDECLARABLE: scripts/synthesis_qa.py has VOICE_LABELS entry 'Cyril' with _LABEL_RE requiring a colon straight after the label, so the catena head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' matches nothing, split_voices() never reports him, and undeclarable_voices() rejects every spelling. Second chapter in a row where this forced SILENT_BY_ENTRY instead of excluded_voices (cf. 1corinthians 1). The VOICE_LABELS list wants an owner decision.

Scraped StudyLight page chrome, 926 words, attached to the Ellicott block at 22:30 - his last block in the chapter, consistent with the attachment model established at galatians 4:30 (chrome attaches to the voice's last block, not the chapter's last verse). Reported usable source was 36,246 words; real usable is ~35,320. Robertson's block follows the chrome intact and was used.

Seven entries, all self-graded verse by verse against the catena: 1-5 648w, 6-11 603w, 12-16 645w, 17-21 650w, 22-24 646w, 25-29 644w, 30 499w. No claim in the prose is unsourced; every named voice has a head in its own span. Entry 6-11 landed in window on the first draft (7 voices, thin source); the four 8-voice entries each needed two to three trim passes, confirming again that overshoot scales with voice count and source density rather than chapter length. Romans 1:32 in entry 17-21 linked as a .ref per the validator.

JFB stride residue, unbroken again: the SAME Numbers 33 itinerary block (Wady Sheikh, Jebel-et-Tih, Hazeroth/Ain-Hadera, the eighteen stations between Hazeroth and Kadesh, Ezion-geber to Kadesh) is filed verbatim at vv.3, 9, 15 and 21 — a perfect stride of six with no gap, the cleanest instance of the pattern seen so far. Nothing in the four blocks touches Deuteronomy 31. All four excluded. The harvest is offset by a fixed step against the verse index and lands wherever that step falls; a harvest-side fix would be to reject a donor block whose scripture references all fall outside the working chapter.

StudyLight chrome tail on the chapter's LAST verse again — v30 carries Ellicott's real note, then the site footer, the CSS block, and the commentary/concordance/dictionary menus. Fourteenth chapter in a row where the tail lands on the final verse. Second-order effect worth naming: the menu text contains the string 'Adam Clarke Commentary', so the ghost checker reported Clarke as PRESENT in the vv.28-30 blob when he has no comment there at all. undeclarable_voices() correctly caught it and left the exclusion list empty, but a chapter where a chrome-only name was NOT auto-detected would produce a spurious exclusion in the tags. Stripping the chrome at harvest fixes both problems at once.

Keil paragraph-boundary defect, twice: his blocks at v15 and v20 are raw quoted verse text (vv.15-19 and vv.20-24 respectively) with no exposition attached. His actual comment on the septennial reading sits at v8, and on the summons of the elders at v25 — one to two verses before the material it treats, the familiar displacement. Both keys excluded. Unlike a Barnes or Gill bare cross-reference, this class IS recoverable by refetching, since the exposition exists and is merely split off at the wrong paragraph boundary.

Median-based entry-count predictor, fourth data point and the sub-800 band confirmed. deuteronomy 31: 22,982 usable source words, 30 keys, median key 647.5, no gaps, nothing over the 4,500 span limit — tiled to NINE entries, i.e. keys divided by 3.3. Running series: leviticus 25 (55 keys, median 457) -> 10 entries, keys/5.5; acts 22 (30 keys, median 696) -> 11, keys/2.7; deuteronomy 31 (30 keys, median 648) -> 9, keys/3.3; genesis 49 (33 keys, median 963) -> 15, keys/2.2; philippians 2 (30 keys, median 1,981) -> projected 15-17, keys/1.9. Word total alone has now mis-signalled workload in both directions five times; the median key is the predictor that tracks. Fourth request that 'synthesis-loop.py size' print the median and a projected entry count beside the word total.

Two filing-rule cases resolved in opposite directions in the same chapter. (1) Clarke's v1 block is the whole-chapter argument — a table of contents running 'Moses, being 120 years old, calls the people together, Deu 31:1-6 ... repeats the song to them, Deu 31:30'. The known displaced-excursus pattern; left unused, and his v2 material on the three forty-year periods carried entry 1 instead. (2) Henry's v14 block is a whole-pericope overview covering vv.14-19, and he has NO key at 16-18. Note 607's rule (use displaced material where the source has a key in the target span) therefore does NOT license moving it; the material was kept in entry 5 where it is filed, which is also what the base filing rule requires. Result: nothing lost, and entry 6 (vv.16-18) legitimately carries no Henry because he is absent from that blob. Worth stating plainly: note 607 is an EXCEPTION for the case where the source has keys on both sides, not a general licence to relocate.

Note 609 (budget items per VOICE before drafting, rather than trimming to the word count afterwards) tested properly for the first time across a whole chapter. Result is mixed but measurable. Two of nine entries landed in range on the FIRST draft with no trim pass at all — v9 at 615 and vv.14-15 at 540, both budgeted item-by-item before a word was written. The other seven still overshot, but by 5-23% rather than the 30-40% that had been usual, and needed 2-6 trim passes instead of 10-19. Where the method failed it failed the same way each time: a paragraph with four or more items from ONE voice (Calvin, always) blew its budget, because the per-item estimate of 90-110 words holds for a single attributed sentence but not for a multi-clause argument with an objection and an answer. Refinement for the next worker: budget a Calvin argument-with-objection at 120-140, not 100, and cap any single voice at three items per entry.

Genuine interpretive crux at v23 worth flagging for anyone reworking this chapter: who speaks 'be strong and of a good courage, for thou shalt bring the children of Israel into the land which I sware unto them'? The nearer antecedent of 'he' is Moses, and the Septuagint translators read it so — but were then forced to emend two clauses, 'the Lord sware' for 'I sware' and 'he shall be with thee' for 'I will be with thee'. Aben Ezra keeps the received text by having Moses speak in God's name and authority. Gill judges for the Lord himself as speaker, and Ellicott independently glosses the subject as Jehovah, calling this the first record of God's direct communion with Joshua. Recorded as an outlier rather than a debate, since no used voice actually HOLDS the Moses reading — it is reported by Gill, not defended by anyone in the catena.

JFB stride residue with a NEW donor chapter, and the cleanest evidence yet for the mechanism. Five keys — vv.4, 10, 16, 22, 28 — a perfect stride of six with no gap, and every one of them carries Deuteronomy 24 material: v4 = the certificate of divorce (24:1-4), v10 = the millstone taken to pledge (24:6), v16 = the poor man's cloak restored before night (24:10-13), v22 = none responsible for the crimes of others (24:16), v28 = the forgotten sheaf and the olive not beaten twice, left for the stranger, fatherless and widow (24:19-21). So the residue is not a single stuck block repeated, as in deuteronomy 31 (where all four keys carried the identical Numbers 33 itinerary): here the donor ADVANCES through its own chapter in step with the stride. That rules out a caching bug and points squarely at a harvest-side index offset — the JFB fetch is walking one source at a fixed step while the verse index walks another. All five excluded.

StudyLight chrome tail on the chapter's LAST verse — v31 carries Ellicott's real note, then the footer, the CSS block and the site menus. Fifteenth chapter in a row where the tail lands on the final verse, and the second in this batch (deuteronomy 31:30 was the fourteenth). Same second-order effect as there: the menu text contains 'Adam Clarke Commentary', so the ghost checker reported Clarke as present in the vv.29-31 blob though he has no comment on those verses; undeclarable_voices() caught it and left the exclusion list empty. The pattern now has enough instances to be treated as deterministic rather than incidental — the harvester is capturing the page tail on whatever request ends the chapter.

Median-based entry-count predictor, fifth data point and the first miss in the sub-800 band. judges 5: 28,618 usable source words, 31 keys, median key 654, no gaps, nothing over the 4,500 span limit — but it tiled to ELEVEN entries, keys/2.8, where deuteronomy 31 (30 keys, median 648, almost identical profile) tiled to nine, keys/3.3. The difference is not the median but the DISTRIBUTION: judges 5 has three heavy keys (v12 at 3,999, v24 at 2,475, v28 at 2,061) sitting among a long tail of 300-800 word keys, so the heavy keys must take spans of their own or near enough, and the light keys cannot be merged far enough to compensate without crossing the 4,500 ceiling. Refinement: the median predicts the count well only when the spread is narrow. A better single number would be the count of keys over ~2,000 words, added to (remaining words / 2,500). For judges 5 that gives 3 + (20,000/2,500) = 11, exactly right; for deuteronomy 31 it gives 0 + (22,982/2,500) = 9, also exactly right. Recommend 'synthesis-loop.py size' print keys-over-2000 and that projection.

Voice profile worth flagging for anyone reworking Judges: this chapter has NO Calvin, NO Wesley, NO Spurgeon and NO Augustine anywhere in its 31 keys. The whole song rests on Gill, Clarke, Ellicott, Keil, and a Henry who has only four keys (vv.1, 6, 12, 24). Consequences for the tags: 'reformed' is Gill alone in every entry and 'wesleyan-arminian' is Clarke alone, so both schools are permanently 'single' prevalence; 'puritan-evangelical' appears in only four of the eleven entries; and 'grammatical-historical' carries Ellicott and Keil together and is the load-bearing school throughout. Ellicott in particular is doing work he does not do elsewhere — he supplies the lexical arguments (perazon, peraoth, the scribe's staff, the dyed robes), the literary parallels (Sir Patrick Spens, Claudian, Gibbon, Aeschylus) and the whole moral discussion of Jael. A chapter this dependent on one commentator is worth re-checking if the Ellicott source is ever refetched.

Four substantive disagreements in this chapter, all recorded in the tags but worth listing together since they are unusually sharp for a single chapter. (1) v2, the word peraoth: Keil argues from the one other occurrence that it means the hairy ones, those who possessed strength, and denies that the sense of leading can be established in Hebrew; Ellicott holds the Septuagint right with 'in the leading of the leaders of Israel' and says the received 'avenging of Israel' is impossible. (2) v4, the march out of Seir: Clarke and Keil take it for Sinai and the giving of the law; Ellicott argues that the mention of Seir and Edom, and the different imagery, require the march from Kadesh Barnea to the first conquest east of Jordan. (3) v24, whether the blessing on Jael approves the deed: Clarke narrows 'bless' to 'praise, celebrate' and denies divine approbation; Ellicott concedes the deed is indefensible but explains Deborah as the creature of her age, and objects strongly to comparing the words with the angel's salutation to the Virgin; Gill and Henry simply justify her as choosing God's side. (4) v26, whether the piled-up verbs betray a thirst for revenge: Ellicott reports the charge and answers it from ancient moral sensibility, Keil denies it outright and says the repetition only means Sisera was struck dead at a blow. Three of the four are direct Ellicott-versus-Keil exchanges.

Material deliberately not used, recorded so the next worker does not re-decide it. Clarke's block at v28 carries a long quotation from Bishop Lowth's thirteenth Prelection on the mother of Sisera — 'a striking image of maternal solicitude, and of a mind divided between hope and fear' — with Lowth's observation that she dwells not on the slaughter of the enemies or the valour of the victor but, burning with the female love of spoils, on damsels, gold and garments, and that the disappointment of her hope is expressed more strongly by the poem's sudden silence than any colouring of words could paint it; followed by Dodd's quotation of Pelicanus challenging Homer or Virgil to match the song. It is the best single piece of literary criticism in the chapter's whole catena. It was left out because it is filed at v28, inside the vv.26-28 entry, which was already at the 650-word ceiling with Clarke present twice, while Ellicott's own citation of Lowth on the same verses falls in the NEXT entry (vv.29-31) and using both would have templated across the two. If this chapter is ever reworked at a higher word budget, Lowth belongs in it.

Jamieson stride-6 defect, SEVENTEENTH consecutive chapter, and the cleanest instance yet: keys 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 - stride 6 from offset 0, FIVE members, NO gap. All five are headless mid-sentence fragments (12, 17, 88, 32 and 32 words) and all five are on ACTS 8, in narrative order: v6 'showing that they regarded Peter as no more than their own equal'; v12 on the term simony; v18 on Peter and John sent to Samaria, quoting Acts 1:8 and Olshausen on the Ethiopian chamberlain; v24 on the voice within directing Philip (Acts 8:29); v30 on the eunuch's deference to Philip (Acts 8:31). FIFTH chapter with the contiguous-region signature (cf. 1corinthians 1 on Acts 16, deuteronomy 22 on Numbers 27-28, hebrews 12 on Galatians 1-2, acts 22 on Acts 2). A perfect stride with no gap and a single contiguous source region in order is as strong as the evidence can get without a re-fetch of the Jamieson tree.

John Lightfoot chapter-component loss, BOTH of his blocks in this chapter unusable, and in two different ways. (a) 3:1 carries his essay on the catena of vv10-19 - the quotations Jewish interpreters applied to the Gentiles - and it names 'ver.19' explicitly; in-chapter but filed at the wrong verse, and it also carries OCR garbage ('CHA Pay PE'). (b) 3:19 carries his note on ROMANS 8:19-22, opening on 'the earnest expectation of the creature' and working through the phrase 'every creature' in Mark 16:15 and Colossians 1:23 - wrong chapter entirely. Both excluded by entry. Same defect class as 1corinthians 1 (1:6=2:6, 1:8=4:8, 1:13=3:13), 1corinthians 16 (key 55 in a 24-verse chapter) and acts 22:1 (= Acts 23).

Theodoret of Cyrrhus: EMPTY BLOCKS. His entries at 3:9, 3:12 and 3:13 carry the verse lemma alone with no commentary attached - 23, 22 and 21 words, each exactly the KJV text of the verse and nothing more. He has real comment at all 25 of his other keys in this chapter. Dropped silently rather than declared, because he is UNDECLARABLE for the same reason as Cyril of Jerusalem: scripts/synthesis_qa.py VOICE_LABELS holds the bare 'Theodoret', and _LABEL_RE requires a colon straight after the label, so the catena head 'Theodoret of Cyrrhus:' matches nothing and split_voices() never reports him. This is the THIRD voice found to be undeclarable by that regex (Cyril of Jerusalem, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and any other multi-word head whose first token is in the list). The VOICE_LABELS defect now has three confirmed instances and wants an owner decision.

Cyril of Jerusalem's single block in this chapter, filed at 3:25, is a catechetical lecture on the eucharistic table expounding Psalm 23 ('Thou hast prepared a table before me') - nothing to do with the propitiation. Off-topic, dropped silently (undeclarable). His other block, at 3:12, IS apt: it quotes Romans 3:12 verbatim at the end of a survey of human wickedness from Cain through the flood and Sodom to the golden calf, and was used. So the Cyril defect remains per-block rather than global.

Scraped StudyLight page chrome, 984 words, attached to the Ellicott block at 3:31 - his last block in the chapter, consistent with the attachment model established at galatians 4:30 and confirmed at acts 22:30 (chrome attaches to the voice's last block, not the chapter's last verse). Robertson's block follows the chrome intact and was used. Reported usable source was 61,415 words; real usable is ~60,431.

Ten entries, all self-graded verse by verse against the catena: 1-2 638w, 3-4 646w, 5-8 648w, 9-12 649w, 13-18 650w, 19-20 650w, 21-23 643w, 24-25 640w, 26-28 650w, 29-31 637w. No claim in the prose is unsourced; every named voice has a head in its own span. Entry 1-2 landed in window on the first draft at 638w despite carrying nine voices - the first 9-voice entry in the corpus to do so - because it was written to a deliberate 620 target. Every other entry needed one to three trim passes, and the two heaviest spans (19-20 at 8,730 source words and 24-25 at 8,168) each had to be rewritten from five paragraphs to four before they would come down. Confirms again that overshoot tracks voice count and source density, not chapter length.

JFB stride residue again — five keys at vv.4, 10, 16, 22, 28, a perfect stride of six, exactly as in judges 5. The donor content here is the sharpest evidence yet for a fixed-offset walk: vv.4, 10 and 16 all carry Leviticus 27 material and ADVANCE through it in order (the vowed field reverting at jubilee, 27:16-21; the solemn vow with self-imprecation, 27:2; the tithe of the land, 27:30-32), and then at v22 and v28 the donor JUMPS BOOKS and picks up Numbers 1 (the thirteen months since the exodus and the census; the hereditary tribal chiefs and the twelve princes appointed to help take it). A donor that walks forward through its own text and then crosses a book boundary in step is not a cached block and not a mis-keyed file — it is one cursor advancing at a fixed rate against another. Running donor list: numbers 33 (deuteronomy 31), deuteronomy 24 (judges 5), leviticus 27 into numbers 1 (numbers 20). All five keys excluded.

StudyLight chrome tail — and this instance BREAKS the fifteen-chapter 'always the last verse' pattern in an instructive way. The chapter's last verse is 29, but the tail sits on v28, inside Ellicott's block. Ellicott has no note at all on v29. So the chrome does not attach to the chapter's final verse as such: it attaches to the final verse of the COMMENTATOR'S OWN run, which in every previous case happened to coincide with the chapter's last verse because that commentator carried the chapter to its end. This is a better-specified version of the same defect and should make the harvest-side fix easier to write — strip the tail from whatever the last response in each commentator's sequence is, rather than from the chapter's last key.

Wesley at v19 is a bare restatement with no comment: the whole block is 'Said - that is, their messengers replied what here follows.' There is nothing to distil, so he is excluded from the vv.19-22 entry, but undeclarable_voices() does not recognise this class and the exclusion has to be carried explicitly in the tags. This is the third distinct no-content class now on record — the Keil raw-verse-text block (deuteronomy 31), the Barnes/Gill bare cross-reference (acts 22), and now the Wesley one-clause paraphrase that merely repeats the verse's own subject and verb. All three produce a voice that is PRESENT in the blob and unusable in the entry. Worth extending undeclarable_voices() to catch a block whose stripped text is under ~15 words and contains no proper noun or scripture reference.

Entry-count predictor: sixth data point, and the refined formula from note 649 held exactly. numbers 20 has 21,325 usable source words across 29 keys, median 379, no gaps. Three keys exceed 2,000 words (v1 at 4,802, v14 at 2,499, v28 at 2,122) and the remaining 26 keys hold 11,902 words. The formula keys-over-2000 + round(remaining/2500) gives 3 + 5 = 8, and the chapter tiled to exactly 8 entries. The median alone would have predicted far more, since at 379 it is the lowest median in the whole running series. That is now three consecutive chapters where the two-term formula was exact (deuteronomy 31: 0 + 9 = 9; judges 5: 3 + 8 = 11; numbers 20: 3 + 5 = 8) and the median-only rule missed twice. Recommend the two-term formula replace the median guidance, and that 'synthesis-loop.py size' print keys-over-2000 alongside the word total. Note also that v1 at 4,802 words exceeds the 4,500 span ceiling but is a SINGLE key, so it cannot be split; a single over-ceiling key simply becomes its own entry, which is worth stating in the loop doc since the span rule as written implies a split is always possible.

Three real disagreements, all recorded in the tags. (1) v2-3, whom the murmurers mean by 'our brethren who died before the Lord': Ellicott argues for the plague after Korah's insurrection, on the strength of the parallel language and a verb that occurs in that history and in only one other place in the last four books; Keil denies Korah's company outright, since the verb for dying would be wholly inapplicable to being swallowed up or burned, and refers it to those who died one by one over the thirty-seven years. The answer bears on whether the chapter belongs to the third year or the fortieth. (2) v8, which rod was taken 'from before the Lord': Keil, Gill and Ellicott all argue for the rod of Moses (Ellicott decisively, from Aaron's name not appearing until after the rod and from Moses smiting with 'his rod'), while Wesley leaves it open on the ground that the wonder-working rod was probably also laid up in the tabernacle. (3) v12, in what the sin consisted: Clarke enumerates four particulars, Wesley the same two with the qualification that they doubted God's will and not his power, Calvin locates the origin in unbelief and calls the double blow an aggravation rather than a cause, and Keil insists the want of confidence was not actual distrust in God's omnipotence. Four positions on one question is unusual and the tags carry three of them.

Material deliberately not used. Henry's block at v22 is a whole-pericope overview running to the end of the chapter, and he has no key anywhere in vv.23-29, so under the filing rule everything in it had to be used in the vv.19-22 entry or lost. Three of his items were carried there (the double funeral, the displeasure-and-mercy of the summons, the Levitical-priesthood type), but the finest passage was dropped for want of room: Moses stripping Aaron of the garments his own hands had first put on, with the reflection that death will strip us, that naked we came into the world and naked we must go out, and that we shall see little reason to be proud of our clothes or marks of honour; together with the note that installing Eleazar before Aaron died forestalled any rival claim on the priesthood, and Aaron's nunc dimittis on seeing his son preferred and his office secured. Wesley says the naked-we-came part almost word for word at v28, so that thought is not lost to the chapter — it is carried in the vv.28-29 entry under his name instead. The Eleazar-installation and nunc dimittis material is genuinely gone. Second chapter running where a Henry or Clarke whole-pericope block filed at one verse could not fit the entry that owns it; the pattern is now frequent enough to be worth a rule of its own.

JFB stride residue, third chapter running and a fourth distinct donor. Two keys only this time, vv.16 and 22 — still the stride of six — and both carry the SAME Deuteronomy 12 block on hunting and venison (game need no longer be brought to the tabernacle door; the people were now as free in killing domestic cattle as wild animals; the deer of Lebanon, Carmel and Gilead would furnish a plentiful repast). Nothing in it touches Joshua 18. Both excluded. Donor tally across four chapters now: numbers 33 (deuteronomy 31), deuteronomy 24 (judges 5), leviticus 27 advancing into numbers 1 (numbers 20), deuteronomy 12 (joshua 18). Four different donor chapters, three different donor books, one constant stride — which rules out any explanation that depends on the particular donor and leaves only the offset itself.

Entry-count predictor: seventh data point, formula exact for the fourth consecutive chapter. joshua 18 has 12,277 usable source words across 28 keys, median 277, no gaps and nothing over the 4,500 span ceiling. One key exceeds 2,000 words (v1 at 2,339) and the remaining 27 keys hold 9,938. keys-over-2000 + round(remaining/2500) gives 1 + 4 = 5, and the chapter tiled to exactly 5 entries. Running record of the two-term formula: deuteronomy 31 predicted 9 got 9; judges 5 predicted 11 got 11; numbers 20 predicted 8 got 8; joshua 18 predicted 5 got 5. Four for four, across medians from 277 to 654 and totals from 12,000 to 29,000 words. The median-only rule would have been wrong on three of the four. This is now well enough attested to belong in the loop doc rather than in the note stream.

Two clean disagreements, both in the tags.
